laws.title: Distracted Driving — Handheld Device Ban
laws.subtitle: NY Vehicle & Traffic Law §1225-d — 5 points added
laws.fullDescription: New York prohibits all handheld device use while driving including texting, calls, apps. Applies even stopped at red lights.
laws.penalty: 1st offense: $200–$400 + 5 points. 2nd within 18 months: $400–$600. 3rd+: up to $600.
exceptions: Emergency 911 calls
Hands-free operation

quiz.q: Points added to NY license for first handheld device violation?
quiz.explanation: A first handheld device violation adds 5 points to your New York license.

laws.title: NYC Rent Stabilization
laws.subtitle: Rent Guidelines Board — 2.75% (1yr) / 5.25% (2yr) for 2024
laws.fullDescription: NYC rent stabilization covers ~1 million apartments. The 2024 Rent Guidelines Board approved 2.75% for one-year leases and 5.25% for two-year leases. Tenants have right to renew.
laws.penalty: Overcharges: repayment plus triple damages for willful violations.
exceptions: Buildings built after 1974
Owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 6 units

quiz.q: NYC approved rent increase for a 1-year lease in 2024?
quiz.explanation: NYC Rent Guidelines Board approved 2.75% for one-year leases in 2024.

laws.title: New York City Culture — Direct & Fast-paced
laws.subtitle: Walk fast, stand right, don't block the sidewalk
laws.fullDescription: New Yorkers are direct and efficient. Stand on the right side of escalators, walk on the left. Never stop suddenly on a busy sidewalk. Tipping is essential — 20% is standard in restaurants; 15% is considered low. Hailing a cab or using your phone on the subway is fine. New Yorkers respect directness; small talk with strangers is less common than in other US cities.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — but blocking a busy sidewalk or under-tipping will earn social disapproval.
exceptions: Tourist areas like Times Square are more forgiving of slower walking
Business settings follow professional norms

quiz.q: Standard restaurant tip percentage in New York City?
quiz.explanation: 20% is the standard tip in NYC restaurants; 15% is considered below average.

laws.title: Cannabis — Legal in NYC; Complex State Rules
laws.subtitle: MRTA 2021 — Adults 21+ may possess 3oz; licensed shops open
laws.fullDescription: New York legalised recreational cannabis in 2021 (Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act). Adults 21+ may legally possess up to 3 ounces of cannabis or 24g of concentrate. Licensed dispensaries are open in NYC. Smoking cannabis is permitted anywhere tobacco smoking is allowed — including sidewalks — but not in cars, workplaces, or near schools. Employers can no longer test most employees for cannabis. However, federal law still prohibits cannabis near federal buildings, airports, and in federal housing.
laws.penalty: Possession over 3oz: civil fine. Public smoking near school: fine. Under-21 possession: civil fine + required education programme.
exceptions: Federally subsidised housing: still prohibited
Federal buildings, airports: prohibited
Under-21: possession is a civil (not criminal) offence
laws.sourceLabel: Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act 2021 — New York

quiz.q: How much cannabis can an adult 21+ legally carry in New York State?
quiz.explanation: New York adults 21+ may legally possess up to 3 ounces of cannabis — legalised under the Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act 2021.

laws.title: NYC Noise Code — One of America's Strictest
laws.subtitle: NYC Administrative Code §24-218 — Night hours 10pm–7am
laws.fullDescription: New York City has a comprehensive Noise Code (NYC Administrative Code Title 24). Construction is prohibited between 10pm and 7am (weekdays) without a special permit. Residential noise complaints between neighbours are handled by 311. Car alarms sounding for more than 3 minutes are a noise violation. Sound levels from bars and restaurants have decibel limits enforced by DEP. Loud music from vehicles is prohibited. Ice cream trucks and street vendors must keep music below 45 decibels.
laws.penalty: Construction without night permit: $350–$2,500. Excessive residential noise: warning then $100+ fine. Car alarm: $350 fine.
exceptions: Emergency construction with DEP permit
Emergency vehicles
laws.sourceLabel: NYC Noise Code — Department of Environmental Protection

quiz.q: What time does NYC's Noise Code prohibit construction work until each morning?
quiz.explanation: NYC's Noise Code prohibits construction between 10pm and 7am on weekdays — construction outside these hours requires a special night work permit from the city.

laws.title: NYC Subway Rules — Turnstile Jumping and Panhandling
laws.subtitle: NY Penal Law §165.15 — Fare evasion; MTA Bylaw on solicitation
laws.fullDescription: New York's MTA subway has strict rules actively enforced. Fare evasion (jumping turnstiles or 'back-door' bus entry) has been a major enforcement priority — over 40 million fare evasions occur annually costing over $700 million. Since 2022, NYPD increased visible subway enforcement. Eating and drinking are technically prohibited on the subway (rarely enforced for food but enforced for alcohol). Panhandling on subway cars is illegal under MTA bylaws. Riding between subway cars while the train is in motion is prohibited. Backpacks must be searched at random checkpoints after high-alert events.
laws.penalty: Fare evasion: criminal or civil summons — up to $100 fine or arrest. Subway car panhandling: $25 fine. Riding between cars: $75 fine.
exceptions: Transit workers and law enforcement
MetroCard or OMNY contactless payment counts as fare payment
laws.sourceLabel: MTA Rules of Conduct — New York

quiz.q: What is turnstile jumping on the NYC subway legally classified as?
options: A misdemeanor only if caught twice
Fare evasion — a criminal or civil offence
quiz.explanation: Jumping NYC subway turnstiles is fare evasion — classified as a criminal or civil offence with up to $100 fine or arrest, and a major enforcement priority costing the MTA $700+ million annually.

laws.title: NYC E-Bike and E-Scooter Laws — Registration, Helmets and Sidewalk Bans
laws.subtitle: NYC Local Law 2021 — Throttle e-bikes banned; Class 1–3 rules apply
laws.fullDescription: New York City dramatically expanded e-bike and e-scooter access with Local Laws enacted 2021–2023, but with important restrictions: throttle-only e-bikes (Class 2, no pedalling required) and Class 3 e-bikes (over 25mph) are banned on NYC streets. Class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes up to 20mph are legal. E-scooters are allowed in select boroughs (not Manhattan) with a pilot programme. Riding any e-bike or e-scooter on the sidewalk is illegal. Riders under 18 must wear a DOT-approved helmet. Electric scooters and e-bikes used for delivery must be registered with DSNY. Lithium-ion battery fires (from unsafe e-bike chargers) are a serious safety issue — NYC has banned non-listed chargers.
laws.penalty: Riding e-bike on sidewalk: $100–300 fine. Unregistered commercial e-bike: $250–500. Non-compliant lithium battery charger: equipment confiscation.
exceptions: Class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes (up to 20mph) are fully legal in all five boroughs
DOT-approved shared e-scooter operators in permitted areas
laws.sourceLabel: NYC Department of Consumer Affairs — E-Bike and Scooter Rules

quiz.q: Which class of e-bike is BANNED on New York City streets because it uses throttle-only with no pedalling required?
quiz.explanation: Class 2 e-bikes (throttle-only, no pedalling required, up to 20mph) are banned on NYC streets — only Class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes are permitted, because they require active pedalling to engage the motor.

laws.title: Broadway Rules — TKTS Booths; Camera Laws in Theatres; Public Performance Permits
laws.subtitle: NYC Cultural Affairs — Photography banned in theatres; busking requires permit
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Broadway theatre scene is the world's most famous — but attending shows comes with strict rules. Recording any performance (audio or video) is illegal under US copyright law and theatre rules — violators are ejected and cameras are confiscated. Mobile phones must be switched off (not silenced). The TKTS booth in Times Square sells same-day discount tickets legitimately — street ticket scalpers are illegal in New York (anti-scalping law, NY Arts and Cultural Affairs §25.03). Street performers (buskers) in the NYC subway require an Arts for Transit permit through MTA's MUNY programme. Performing without a permit in Central Park or public plazas requires NYC Parks approval. Times Square's costumed characters (Elmo, Spider-Man) are legal but tips must be consensual.
laws.penalty: Recording a Broadway show: ejection + copyright infringement — civil damages. Illegal ticket scalping: Class A misdemeanor. Unlicensed busking in subway: $50 fine.
exceptions: Press photographers at media preview performances with theatre PR accreditation
MUNY-permitted subway performers

quiz.q: What is the name of New York's MTA programme that licenses legitimate subway buskers/performers?
quiz.explanation: MTA's MUNY (Music Under New York) programme issues permits to subway performers through auditions — licensed MUNY performers can legally busk at designated subway stations, while unlicensed performers can be fined.

laws.title: NYC Rent Stabilization — Strict Limits on Rent Increases in Regulated Apartments
laws.subtitle: Over 1 million NYC apartments have rent-increase caps; landlord violations carry heavy penalties
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Rent Stabilization Law (Administrative Code §26-501) covers approximately 1 million apartments built before 1974. Landlords of stabilized units can only raise rents by percentages set annually by the Rent Guidelines Board. The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act eliminated many pathways to deregulate units, including the former vacancy bonus and luxury decontrol. Preferential rents (below-legal rents given to tenants) are now locked in — landlords cannot raise to the legal maximum if they previously charged less. Landlords must renew leases of stabilized tenants and cannot evict without just cause. Lease riders must disclose stabilized status. Violating rent laws: tenants can file complaints with DHCR (Division of Housing and Community Renewal) for rent overcharges.
laws.penalty: Rent overcharge: mandatory repayment of 2 years of overcharges. Willful overcharge (fraud): triple damages (3x the overcharge amount) going back 6 years. Illegal eviction: fines + criminal trespass charges.
exceptions: Buildings with fewer than 6 units may be exempt
Units built after 1974 (absent other programs) are generally market-rate
Section 8 voucher units have different federal subsidy rules
laws.sourceLabel: NYS DHCR — Rent Stabilization Law Guide

quiz.q: What happened to preferential rents in NYC after the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act?
options: They were abolished — all tenants must pay legal maximum
They were locked in — landlords cannot raise to legal maximum if they previously charged less
They were increased by 10% as a landlord incentive
They became negotiable on a building-by-building basis
quiz.explanation: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act locked in preferential rents — if a landlord had been charging below the legal maximum, they cannot suddenly raise it to the maximum at lease renewal. This closed a major loophole that had allowed destabilization of many apartments.

laws.title: NYC Landmarks Preservation Law — Strictest Historic Building Protections in USA
laws.subtitle: NYC's 1965 law protects 37,000+ buildings; demolition or alteration requires LPC approval
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Landmarks Preservation Law (1965) — passed after the 1963 demolition of the magnificent Pennsylvania Station shocked the public — created the Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC). Over 37,000 buildings and sites are designated individually or within historic districts. Owners of landmarked properties must obtain LPC approval for any exterior alterations — including window replacement, storefronts, and façade painting. Interior landmarks (like Grand Central Terminal's main concourse) have additional interior protections. Demolition of a landmark requires extraordinary justification. The law has been tested repeatedly: Grand Central Terminal was saved from a skyscraper above it in Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (1978, US Supreme Court upheld law). The law applies regardless of private property ownership.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized alteration of landmark exterior: stop-work orders + fines up to $100,000. Illegal demolition of landmark: criminal prosecution under City Charter + fines up to $500,000 + mandatory reconstruction.
exceptions: Emergency repairs with LPC notification within 24 hours
Non-visible interior modifications (LPC reviews only exterior and designated interiors)
Tax incentives reduce compliance cost burden for owners of designated buildings
laws.sourceLabel: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission — Landmark Law

quiz.q: What major New York City building demolition in 1963 shocked the public and prompted the creation of NYC's Landmarks Preservation Law?
quiz.explanation: The 1963 demolition of Pennsylvania Station — a magnificent Beaux-Arts structure modeled on Rome's Caracalla Baths — shocked New York City and prompted the creation of the Landmarks Preservation Law in 1965. Architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable wrote: 'We will probably be judged not by the monuments we build but by those we have destroyed.'

laws.title: Stop-and-Frisk Unconstitutional Ruling
laws.subtitle: Federal court ruled NYPD racial profiling violated 4th and 14th Amendments
laws.fullDescription: In Floyd v. City of New York (2013), Federal Judge Shira Scheindlin ruled that the NYPD's stop-and-frisk program constituted unconstitutional racial profiling, violating both the 4th Amendment (unreasonable searches) and 14th Amendment (equal protection). Between 2003–2013, over 4.4 million stops were conducted; 88% involved Black or Latino individuals. Mayor Bloomberg appealed but incoming Mayor de Blasio dropped the appeal in 2014, accepting court-mandated reforms. The ruling required a federal monitor and new training protocols.
laws.penalty: Unconstitutional stops expose city to civil liability. Officers conducting racially-motivated stops face disciplinary action and potential federal civil rights charges.
exceptions: Terry stops remain lawful when officer has reasonable articulable suspicion
Brief investigatory stops based on specific behaviors are permissible
Voluntary consensual encounters do not require justification
laws.sourceLabel: Center for Constitutional Rights — Floyd v. NYC

quiz.q: What did the 2013 Floyd v. City of New York ruling find about stop-and-frisk?
quiz.explanation: Federal Judge Shira Scheindlin ruled NYPD stop-and-frisk violated the 4th and 14th Amendments through systematic racial profiling of Black and Latino New Yorkers.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing — Launched & Frozen
laws.subtitle: NYC launched the US's first congestion pricing zone in June 2024, then Governor Cuomo froze it
laws.fullDescription: New York City launched the United States' first congestion pricing program on June 30, 2024, charging most drivers $9 to enter Manhattan below 60th Street — aiming to reduce traffic, cut emissions, and raise $1 billion annually for subway and bus upgrades. The program was 15 years in the making after state legislation in 2019. However, Governor Kathy Hochul 'paused' the program just 14 days before launch — citing economic concerns for drivers during high inflation — then finally launched it June 30, 2024. Congestion fell 8% in the first months. Opponents sued, and legal battles continued over the environmental review process.
laws.penalty: Drivers who fail to pay the $9 toll receive violations and fines. Toll evasion: $50–$100 per violation. Emergency vehicles are exempt; taxis pay $2.25 per trip; trucks pay $14.40–$21.60.
exceptions: Drivers with disabilities may apply for exemptions
Emergency vehicles are fully exempt
New Jersey commuters using certain tunnels may receive credits
laws.sourceLabel: MTA — Central Business District Tolling Program

quiz.q: What made New York City's June 2024 congestion pricing program historically significant?
options: It was the world's first congestion pricing zone
It was the first congestion pricing program in the United States
It was the largest tolling zone in history
It was the first program approved by a federal court
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing zone, launched June 30, 2024, was the first congestion pricing program in the United States — charging $9 to enter Manhattan below 60th Street to reduce traffic and fund public transit improvements.

laws.title: NYPD Surveillance & Facial Recognition Debate
laws.subtitle: New York passed a transparency law but rejected bans on NYPD facial recognition
laws.fullDescription: New York City's POST Act (2020) required the NYPD to publish a surveillance technology report — the first major US city transparency requirement for police surveillance tools. The NYPD disclosed it uses facial recognition, cell-site simulators (stingrays), X-ray vans, ShotSpotter gunshot detection, and social media monitoring. Advocates pushed for banning facial recognition; the city council rejected a ban. NYC's Real-Time Crime Center aggregates facial recognition across 18,000 cameras citywide. Several cases of wrongful arrests of Black men due to facial recognition misidentification fueled reform calls. The AI surveillance debate is one of New York's most contested civil liberties issues.
laws.penalty: Wrongful arrest based on facial recognition misidentification: civil liability for the city. Illegal surveillance without warrant: evidence exclusion and civil rights claims. Unauthorized use of surveillance data: potential criminal charges under wiretapping laws.
exceptions: The POST Act requires disclosure but does not limit NYPD surveillance powers
Certain counter-terrorism operations using surveillance are classified
Undercover operations using surveillance tools have separate warrant requirements

quiz.q: What did New York City's POST Act (2020) require the NYPD to do?
options: Obtain a warrant before using surveillance cameras
Publish a report disclosing all surveillance technologies used
quiz.explanation: New York City's POST Act (2020) required the NYPD to publish a surveillance technology report disclosing all the surveillance tools it uses — the first major US city transparency requirement for police surveillance, revealing facial recognition, cell-site simulators, ShotSpotter, and more.

laws.title: Rikers Island: Federal Oversight & Closure Mandate
laws.subtitle: New York's notorious Rikers Island jail is under federal receiver control after a decade of deaths and abuse
laws.fullDescription: Rikers Island, New York City's main jail complex, has been under federal monitoring since 2015 after a DOJ investigation found a 'culture of violence' against detained young men. Deaths in custody reached 19 in 2022 — the highest in decades — triggering federal judges to impose ever-tighter oversight. In 2022, a federal monitor found the city was not complying with a consent decree. In 2023, a federal judge threatened to appoint a receiver to take direct control from the city. New York City committed to closing Rikers by 2027 and replacing it with four borough-based jails. The closure deadline has been repeatedly pushed back.
laws.penalty: Specific to facility management: city officials risk contempt of court for non-compliance with federal orders. No individual criminal charges have been filed for most in-custody deaths
exceptions: Persons sentenced to state prison are transferred out of city jails — Rikers holds pre-trial detainees and those serving sentences under one year
LGBTQ+ detainees have a dedicated housing unit with different protocols
laws.sourceLabel: NYC Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice – Rikers Closure

quiz.q: By what year did New York City commit to closing Rikers Island jail?
quiz.explanation: New York City committed to closing Rikers Island by 2027, replacing it with four borough-based jails. The deadline has been pushed back repeatedly, and the federal court has threatened receiver control due to ongoing constitutional violations.

laws.title: NYC Congestion Pricing: America's First — Then Paused — Urban Toll Zone
laws.subtitle: New York launched the US's first congestion pricing zone in 2024, then Governor Hochul abruptly paused it days before implementation
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Central Business District Tolling Program — the first congestion pricing scheme in the United States — was signed into law in 2019 and authorized tolls on vehicles entering Manhattan below 60th Street to reduce traffic and fund the MTA. After years of delays, the program was set to launch on June 30, 2024, with tolls of $9–$23 per vehicle depending on type. Governor Hochul abruptly paused the program on June 5, 2024 — just three weeks before launch — citing economic concerns post-pandemic. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority sued, arguing only the legislature could halt the approved program. A federal judge upheld the pause in December 2024. The program's fate remained uncertain in 2025.
laws.penalty: Driving in a tolling zone without paying: fines plus toll charges. MTA enforcement via license plate cameras
exceptions: Certain emergency vehicles, tunnel and bridge workers, and low-income drivers had reduced or exempted toll rates
The program includes credits for drivers who already pay MTA bridge and tunnel tolls
laws.sourceLabel: MTA – Central Business District Tolling Program

quiz.q: What made New York City's congestion pricing program historically significant?
options: It was the world's first congestion pricing program
It was the largest toll system ever built
It was the first congestion pricing program in the United States
It was the first toll road in New York State
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing program would have been the first in the United States — decades after similar programs launched in London (2003), Stockholm (2006), and Singapore (1975). Governor Hochul's last-minute pause made the US's first congestion pricing scheme the most anticipated — and most controversial — urban toll zone in American history.

laws.title: Rent Stabilisation Law
laws.subtitle: New York's rent stabilisation caps rent increases on millions of apartments
laws.fullDescription: New York's Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA 2019) dramatically strengthened rent stabilization rules covering approximately one million apartments in New York City. Rent increases for stabilized apartments are set annually by the Rent Guidelines Board (typically 2–4%). The 2019 law eliminated 'vacancy bonuses' (landlords could no longer raise rent by 20% when a tenant left), eliminated 'luxury deregulation' (apartments can no longer exit stabilization regardless of rent level), and made it much harder to convert stabilized apartments to market rate through major capital improvements. New York also has a separate Rent Control system covering pre-1947 buildings.
laws.penalty: Landlords who overcharge stabilized tenants: repayment of up to 3 years of overcharges plus treble damages (triple the overcharge); loss of stabilization status
exceptions: Buildings with fewer than 6 units and newer construction are generally not subject to stabilization
Owner-occupied buildings of 2–4 units may be exempt
laws.sourceLabel: New York Homes and Community Renewal

quiz.q: Approximately how many apartments in New York City are covered by rent stabilization?
quiz.explanation: Approximately one million apartments in New York City are covered by rent stabilization — a crucial affordability protection in one of the world's most expensive rental markets.

laws.title: Stop and Frisk Reform
laws.subtitle: New York's stop-and-frisk was declared unconstitutional racial profiling
laws.fullDescription: New York City's police 'stop-and-frisk' policy — allowing officers to temporarily detain and search any person they 'reasonably suspected' — peaked at 685,724 stops in 2011, with over 85% of those stopped being Black or Latino. In Floyd v. City of New York (2013), Federal Judge Shira Scheindlin ruled that NYPD's stop-and-frisk practices violated the 4th Amendment (unreasonable search) and 14th Amendment (equal protection) of the US Constitution. She ordered a federal monitor and reforms. Stops dropped dramatically after the ruling. The case became a landmark in policing reform jurisprudence and influenced similar reform efforts nationwide.
laws.penalty: N/A — this ruling restricted police authority; individual officers who conduct unconstitutional stops face civil liability and disciplinary action
exceptions: Terry stops (limited to the reasonable suspicion standard set in Terry v. Ohio) remain constitutional — the issue was the NYPD's racial bias in application
laws.sourceLabel: Center for Constitutional Rights – Floyd v. NYC

quiz.q: What percentage of those stopped under NYPD's stop-and-frisk were Black or Latino?
quiz.explanation: Over 85% of the 685,724 people stopped by NYPD under stop-and-frisk in 2011 were Black or Latino — a racial disparity that Federal Judge Scheindlin found violated constitutional equal protection rights in the 2013 Floyd v. NYC ruling.

laws.title: Times Square Pedestrian Plazas
laws.subtitle: New York's Times Square was redesigned as a pedestrian zone through city code changes
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Times Square pedestrianization — implemented permanently in 2009 after a 2009 pilot — closed Broadway between 42nd and 47th Streets to cars, creating pedestrian plazas. The change required amendments to New York City's traffic code and coordination with the NYC Department of Transportation. Studies showed pedestrian injuries fell 40%, retail rents increased, and tourist activity boomed. The pedestrian zones also created the legal space for 'costumed characters' (Elmo, Spider-Man, etc.) who tip for photos — a practice that generated complaints and a 2016 regulation designating specific 'activity zones' where they must stay.
laws.penalty: Driving in the pedestrianized zone: traffic violation fines; costumed characters outside designated activity zones: civil summonses
exceptions: Emergency vehicles and delivery vehicles during designated hours have limited access
NYPD and city vehicles have permanent access
laws.sourceLabel: New York City Department of Transportation

quiz.q: By how much did pedestrian injuries fall after Times Square was pedestrianized?
quiz.explanation: After the permanent pedestrianization of Times Square in 2009, pedestrian injuries in the area fell by approximately 40% — demonstrating that removing cars from a heavily trafficked tourist district can significantly improve pedestrian safety.

laws.title: Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA)
laws.subtitle: New York's 2019 climate law set the most ambitious statutory emissions targets in the world at the time
laws.fullDescription: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), signed July 18, 2019, is one of the world's most ambitious statutory climate laws. Key targets: 70% renewable electricity by 2030; 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040; 85% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 from 1990 levels; zero net greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The law created the Climate Action Council (40 members) to develop the Scoping Plan for achieving these goals. A landmark 'environmental justice' provision requires 35-40% of clean energy benefits to flow to disadvantaged communities. The CLCPA mandates offshore wind development (9,000 megawatts by 2035), distributed solar (10,000 megawatts by 2030), and pumped hydropower. Implementation has faced challenges: the 2023 offshore wind crisis saw developers cancel contracts due to inflation and supply chain issues. The law was the first in the U.S. to include a binding greenhouse gas emissions cap with legal penalties for non-compliance.
laws.penalty: State agencies that violate CLCPA requirements face legal action; enforcement through the Department of Environmental Conservation; industry violations of the emissions cap: regulatory sanctions
exceptions: Agricultural emissions have a separate, more lenient pathway
Existing nuclear plants receive zero-emission credits
Emergency power generation has temporary exemptions during grid emergencies

laws.title: Congestion Pricing for Manhattan (2019 Law, 2025 Implementation)
laws.subtitle: New York became the first US city to implement congestion pricing, then paused it amid political controversy
laws.fullDescription: New York's Traffic Mobility Act (2019) authorized the nation's first urban congestion pricing program — charging vehicles a fee to enter Manhattan's central business district (south of 60th Street). The proceeds fund the MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority). After years of environmental review and federal approval, the program was set to launch in June 2024. Governor Kathy Hochul paused the program indefinitely in June 2024, citing economic concerns (COVID recovery, small business impacts) and political pressures from suburban Congressional Democrats. The pause was immediately challenged in federal court — by the MTA, transit advocates, and environmental groups — as a violation of the federal environmental review process. A federal judge ruled the pause was unlawful and ordered implementation; the case went to the 2nd Circuit. The congestion charge would have been $9 per private car. The program was ultimately relaunched in January 2025 under court order, making New York the first US city to implement congestion pricing.
laws.penalty: Vehicles entering the congestion zone without paying: violation penalty plus the toll; repeat violations: license plate-based collection enforcement
exceptions: Emergency vehicles are exempt
Residents of the Manhattan CBD earning under $60,000/year received a tax credit
Certain tunnels (Hugh L. Carey) had toll credits applied against the congestion fee
Trucks have separate pricing tiers

laws.title: NYC Congestion Pricing Pause and Legal Battle
laws.subtitle: Governor Hochul paused congestion pricing hours before it launched
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Central Business District Tolling Program — the first congestion pricing scheme in the US — was set to charge drivers $15 to enter Manhattan south of 60th Street starting June 30, 2024. Hours before launch, Governor Kathy Hochul announced an indefinite pause, citing economic concerns. The MTA had already spent hundreds of millions implementing the program, and the toll revenues were meant to fund $15 billion in transit upgrades. Lawsuits were filed by transit advocates and the federal government sought review. The decision drew condemnation from environmental and transportation groups. Legal battles over reinstatement continued through 2025.
laws.penalty: Driving in the Congestion Zone without paying (if implemented): $50–$100 fine per violation. Toll evasion repeated offenses: escalating fines.
exceptions: Emergency vehicles exempt
Certain low-income drivers eligible for reduced rates under MTA's credit program
Residents of the CBD earning below income threshold get tax credit
laws.sourceLabel: MTA – Central Business District Tolling Program

quiz.q: Why did Governor Hochul pause NYC's congestion pricing in June 2024?
options: Federal regulators found environmental review incomplete
She cited economic concerns, just hours before the program was to launch
A court injunction blocked the program
quiz.explanation: Governor Hochul cited economic concerns and paused the program indefinitely just hours before drivers were to be charged $15 to enter Manhattan below 60th Street.

laws.title: Good Cause Eviction Law – New York 2024
laws.subtitle: New York State enacted landmark renter protections limiting evictions statewide
laws.fullDescription: New York State's Good Cause Eviction Law, enacted in April 2024 as part of the state budget, extended tenant protections beyond New York City's rent-stabilized units. It limits evictions to specific 'good cause' reasons (non-payment of rent, lease violation, owner occupancy) and caps rent increases at the lower of 10% or 5% plus CPI for covered tenants. The law covers most non-luxury market-rate tenants across the state. Landlords argued it would reduce housing investment; tenant advocates called it a historic protection against displacement. The law allowed localities to opt in, and New York City automatically became covered. It represented the biggest expansion of tenant rights since the 1970s.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction without good cause: civil damages up to 3x monthly rent. Harassment to force tenant departure: additional civil and criminal penalties under RPL §768.
exceptions: Buildings with fewer than 4 units where owner lives in one unit exempt
Luxury units above substantial rent threshold exempt
Tenants who have lived in unit less than 1 year have reduced protections
laws.sourceLabel: New York State Senate – Good Cause

quiz.q: What does New York's Good Cause Eviction Law limit?
options: The number of apartments a single landlord may own
Evictions to specific legally defined reasons, and rent increases to 10% or 5%+CPI
Airbnb-style short-term rentals in residential buildings
New condo conversions from rental buildings
quiz.explanation: New York's Good Cause Eviction Law limits evictions to specific causes (non-payment, lease violations, owner occupancy) and caps rent increases at the lower of 10% or 5% plus inflation — the biggest expansion of tenant rights since the 1970s.

laws.title: New York Passes Equal Rights Amendment Including Abortion
laws.subtitle: New York enshrined reproductive rights in the state constitution
laws.fullDescription: In November 2024, New York voters approved a constitutional Equal Rights Amendment (Prop 1) that added expanded protections against discrimination based on ethnicity, national origin, age, disability, and sex — explicitly including 'pregnancy, pregnancy outcomes, and reproductive healthcare and autonomy.' This effectively enshrined abortion rights in the New York state constitution, providing protection beyond the federal constitutional framework weakened by Dobbs. New York joined several other states (including California and Vermont) in embedding reproductive rights in state constitutions. The amendment also strengthened age and disability discrimination protections. Opponents argued it was ambiguous and could have unintended consequences.
laws.penalty: Violations of constitutional equal rights protections: civil rights suits and government liability. State agencies discriminating: civil rights enforcement by Attorney General.
exceptions: Religious institutions retain some exemptions from anti-discrimination law
Private employers' reasonable accommodations for pregnancy included in protections

quiz.q: What reproductive rights language did New York's 2024 Equal Rights Amendment include?
options: A right to free contraception for all residents
Protection against discrimination based on 'pregnancy, pregnancy outcomes, and reproductive healthcare and autonomy'
An explicit right to abortion until 24 weeks
A prohibition on any restriction on reproductive healthcare
quiz.explanation: New York's 2024 ERA added explicit protection against discrimination based on 'pregnancy, pregnancy outcomes, and reproductive healthcare and autonomy' — effectively enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution without naming 'abortion' directly.

laws.title: New York's Wrongful Death Damages Reform
laws.subtitle: NY expanded wrongful death recovery to include grief and non-economic losses
laws.fullDescription: New York's Grieving Families Act (signed 2023) amended the wrongful death statute to expand who can recover damages and what damages are available. Previously, New York was unusual in allowing only economic damages (lost earnings, medical bills) in wrongful death cases — no recovery for grief, loss of companionship, or emotional suffering. The reform expanded the list of eligible family members who can bring claims to include parents, siblings, and domestic partners, and explicitly allows recovery for grief and anguish. The law was several years in the making, driven by COVID-19 wrongful death cases.
laws.penalty: The law creates civil liability — not criminal penalties. Defendants in wrongful death cases now face potential liability for non-economic losses like grief and loss of companionship in addition to economic damages. Statute of limitations: 2.5 years from date of death
exceptions: The changes apply prospectively — pre-enactment deaths follow old law
Medical malpractice wrongful death claims have additional procedural requirements
Government immunity rules still limit some wrongful death claims against state agencies
laws.sourceLabel: New York State Senate - Grieving Families Act

quiz.q: What was the main limitation of New York's old wrongful death law that the 2023 reform addressed?
options: Only economic damages were allowed — no recovery for grief or emotional suffering
Statute of limitations was too short
quiz.explanation: New York was unusual among states in limiting wrongful death recovery to economic losses only — no compensation for grief, loss of companionship, or emotional suffering. The 2023 Grieving Families Act added these non-economic damages.

laws.title: New York's Congestion Pricing Pause
laws.subtitle: MTA's first-in-US congestion pricing program halted by governor
laws.fullDescription: New York City implemented the United States' first congestion pricing program in June 2024 — charging most vehicles $9-$23 to enter Manhattan below 60th Street, with revenue dedicated to MTA public transit improvements. However, Governor Kathy Hochul paused the program indefinitely in June 2024 (days before it was to take effect) citing economic concerns, despite significant investment in infrastructure and planning. The MTA and environmental groups sued to reinstate the program. The pause was a major political controversy — the program had been years in development under a 2019 state law and required federal approval.
laws.penalty: Driving in the Manhattan Central Business District without paying toll (once reinstated): fines plus tolls owed. Toll evasion: civil penalties up to $50 per violation. Non-payment escalating fees. Under original law: penalties for violations of Clean Air requirements that the program was designed to address
exceptions: Emergency vehicles exempt from congestion charge
Residents below median income thresholds receive tax credits
Vehicles with disabled parking placards have modified charges
laws.sourceLabel: MTA - Central Business District Tolling Program

quiz.q: What was historically significant about New York City's June 2024 congestion pricing program?
options: It was the world's first congestion pricing scheme
It was the first congestion pricing program in the United States
It was the most expensive congestion charge in the world
It was the first program to use dynamic pricing
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing program was the first in the United States — charging drivers to enter Manhattan's central business district, with revenue dedicated to MTA transit improvements, though Governor Hochul controversially paused it days before implementation.

laws.title: NYC Tenant Protection and Rent Stabilization Laws
laws.subtitle: New York's rent stabilization system provides strong tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 significantly strengthened tenant rights under the rent stabilization system. Landlords of rent-stabilized apartments face strict limits on rent increases, renovation evictions, and high-income deregulation. Illegal evictions (lockouts, utility shutoffs, harassment) are class A misdemeanors. The 2024 Good Cause Eviction Law extended protections to many previously unregulated tenants. Both tenants and landlords must understand their legal obligations. Failure to provide required notices or illegally evicting tenants can result in treble damages.
laws.penalty: Illegal lockout or harassment: fines up to $10,000 per day; illegal eviction: criminal prosecution as Class A misdemeanor
exceptions: Owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 4 units
Luxury units above specific rent thresholds after proper deregulation

quiz.q: What did NYC's 2019 Housing Stability Act do to rent-stabilized apartments?
options: Strengthened tenant protections and limited rent increases
Reduced the number of stabilized units
quiz.explanation: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act significantly strengthened NYC tenant rights, limiting rent increases and making various landlord practices illegal.

laws.title: Freelance Isn't Free Act Expansion
laws.subtitle: New York expanded protections for freelancers and gig workers in 2023
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Freelance Isn't Free Act (2017), the first of its kind nationally, required written contracts for freelance work over $800, guaranteed payment within 30 days, and prohibited retaliation. In 2023, New York State expanded similar protections statewide with the New York Freelance Isn't Free Act. Clients who fail to pay freelancers face double damages plus attorney fees. The New York Department of Labor enforces the law and can file suit on behalf of freelancers. The law covers any person hired as an independent contractor for services valued at $800 or more, either in a single contract or in aggregate over 120 days.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay freelancer: double the amount owed plus attorney fees; failure to provide written contract: civil penalties
exceptions: Sales representatives covered under separate Sales Representative Act
Lawyers and licensed professionals may have overlapping protections under their licensing rules

quiz.q: What must New York clients provide to freelancers for work valued at $800 or more?
quiz.explanation: New York's Freelance Isn't Free Act requires written contracts for freelance work valued at $800 or more (individually or in aggregate over 120 days), protecting freelancers' payment rights.

laws.title: Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
laws.subtitle: New York's CLCPA targets 100% clean electricity by 2040
laws.fullDescription: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), signed in 2019, is one of the most ambitious climate laws in the US. It mandates 70% renewable electricity by 2030, 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040, and an 85% reduction in economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The law uniquely requires 35-40% of climate investment benefits to flow to disadvantaged communities. The Climate Action Council developed a Scoping Plan guiding implementation. New York is pursuing offshore wind, solar, and energy storage to meet targets. Non-compliance with utility procurement targets can result in Public Service Commission orders and financial penalties.
laws.penalty: Utility non-compliance with renewable purchase obligations: Public Service Commission fines and mandatory compliance orders
exceptions: Small distributed generation under specific output thresholds
Emergency reliability provisions allowing short-term use of non-qualifying resources
laws.sourceLabel: New York State Climate Action Council

quiz.q: What unique social equity requirement does New York's CLCPA include?
options: Free EV charging for low-income residents
35-40% of climate investment benefits must flow to disadvantaged communities
Climate jobs guaranteed to union workers only
quiz.explanation: New York's CLCPA uniquely requires that 35-40% of the benefits from climate investments flow to disadvantaged communities — a social equity provision embedded directly into the climate law.

laws.title: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools
laws.subtitle: NYC law regulates AI hiring tools used by employers
laws.fullDescription: New York City Local Law 144 requires employers using automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) to conduct annual bias audits by independent third parties and publish the results. Job applicants and employees must be notified when an AEDT is used to evaluate them. The law applies to tools that use machine learning or AI to assess candidates for hire or promotion.
laws.penalty: Fines of $375–$1,500 per violation for employers who fail to audit or disclose AEDT use
exceptions: Tools that are not automated (manual scoring)
Positions outside NYC
Tools used only for scheduling, not evaluation

quiz.q: What does New York City Local Law 144 require of employers using AI hiring tools?
options: Annual bias audits and candidate notification
quiz.explanation: NYC Local Law 144 mandates independent annual bias audits and disclosure to job candidates when AI-based hiring tools are used.

laws.title: New York Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
laws.subtitle: New York's CLCPA is among the most ambitious state climate laws
laws.fullDescription: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA, 2019) sets legally binding targets: 70% renewable electricity by 2030, 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040, and net-zero economy-wide emissions by 2050. Notably, it dedicates 35-40% of clean energy investments to disadvantaged communities. The Climate Action Council developed a comprehensive scoping plan, and sector-specific regulations are being developed. Implementation has faced challenges from gas industry lobbying and permitting delays.
laws.penalty: State agencies that fail to advance CLCPA goals face legal challenges; no direct criminal penalties but administrative enforcement
exceptions: Emergency reliability exceptions for grid stability
Industrial processes with no current zero-carbon alternatives
Agricultural methane under separate voluntary programs

quiz.q: What community equity provision does New York's CLCPA include?
options: All investments go to New York City
35-40% of clean energy investments directed to disadvantaged communities
Investments are distributed equally by population
quiz.explanation: New York's CLCPA requires that 35-40% of clean energy benefits and investments flow to disadvantaged communities, making environmental justice a core legal requirement.

laws.title: New York Concealed Carry Improvement Act
laws.subtitle: New York responds to Supreme Court ruling by tightening gun laws
laws.fullDescription: After the US Supreme Court's Bruen decision (2022) struck down New York's previous concealed carry licensing scheme, New York enacted the Concealed Carry Improvement Act (CCIA). The CCIA requires demonstration of good moral character for concealed carry permits, creates new sensitive locations where carrying is prohibited (including government buildings, parks, churches, bars, and Times Square), and requires training and firearms storage requirements. This law itself was partially struck down by lower courts before being partially upheld.
laws.penalty: Carrying in a sensitive location: class E felony; carrying without valid permit: class A misdemeanor to felony depending on circumstances
exceptions: Law enforcement officers on duty
Retired law enforcement with carry permits
Security personnel with proper licensing

quiz.q: What US Supreme Court decision forced New York to redesign its concealed carry law?
quiz.explanation: The Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle and Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022) struck down New York's previous concealed carry licensing requirements, forcing the state to enact the Concealed Carry Improvement Act.

laws.title: New York Freelance Isn't Free Act Expansion
laws.subtitle: New York strengthens protections for freelance workers
laws.fullDescription: New York's Freelance Isn't Free Act, originally enacted in NYC in 2017, was expanded statewide in 2023. The law requires written contracts for freelance work over $800, mandates payment within 30 days of completing work, prohibits retaliation against freelancers who assert their rights, and creates a private right of action with double damages for violations. New York was the first state to enact comprehensive freelance worker payment protection legislation.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay freelancer: double damages plus attorney fees; retaliation: additional penalties; failure to provide written contract: civil fine
exceptions: Work for a household employer
Single-transaction work below $800
Government contracts follow separate procurement rules

quiz.q: What does New York's Freelance Isn't Free Act require for freelance work over $800?
options: A written contract and payment within 30 days of completion
quiz.explanation: New York's Freelance Isn't Free Act requires written contracts for freelance work valued over $800 and mandates payment within 30 days of completing the work, with double damages for violations.

laws.title: NY SAFE Act Gun Regulations
laws.subtitle: New York's comprehensive assault weapon ban and firearm restrictions
laws.fullDescription: New York's SAFE Act (Secure Ammunition and Firearms Enforcement Act) is among the nation's strictest gun control laws. It banned assault-style weapons and requires registration of previously owned assault weapons, limits ammunition magazines to 7 rounds, requires background checks for all ammunition purchases, mandates mental health reporting to a database checked for gun purchases, requires pistol permit recertification every 5 years, and created a statewide database of ammunition sales. The law was challenged but largely upheld by federal courts.
laws.penalty: Possession of an unregistered assault weapon carries up to 4 years imprisonment; illegal magazine possession carries up to 1 year; failure to safely store firearms accessible to children carries fines
exceptions: Law enforcement officers are exempt from assault weapon ban
Antique firearms and muzzle-loaders have different rules
Licensed dealers may sell AR-15 style rifles with modified features that remove assault weapon classification

quiz.q: What unusual ammunition regulation does New York's SAFE Act require for all purchases?
options: Purchasers must show proof of training
A 7-day waiting period for all ammo
Background checks for all ammunition purchases
Ammunition must be stored in locked containers
quiz.explanation: New York's SAFE Act requires background checks for all ammunition purchases, a requirement that goes beyond federal law which only mandates background checks for firearm purchases.

laws.title: Good Cause Eviction Law
laws.subtitle: New York state's just cause eviction protections for renters
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted a statewide Good Cause Eviction law as part of budget legislation, extending tenant protections beyond New York City. The law requires landlords to have good cause before evicting a tenant — meaning non-payment of rent, lease violations, or other specific grounds. It also limits annual rent increases to 5% plus CPI (capped at 10%) for covered units. The law applies to most market-rate rental units across the state, though buildings built after 2009 are exempt for 30 years and owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 4 units are exempt. New York City already had its own tenant protections.
laws.penalty: Landlords who attempt to evict tenants without good cause face court proceedings and attorneys fees awards; charging rent increases above the allowable cap creates civil liability to tenants
exceptions: Units in owner-occupied small buildings are exempt
New construction built after 2009 is exempt for 30 years
Vacation rentals and seasonal rentals are exempt
Units in cooperative and condominium buildings are exempt

quiz.q: What is the maximum annual rent increase allowed under New York's Good Cause Eviction law?
quiz.explanation: New York's Good Cause Eviction law limits rent increases to 5% plus the local CPI rate, with a maximum cap of 10% per year — meaning if inflation is very high, landlords still cannot raise rents more than 10%.

laws.title: Clean Slate Act
laws.subtitle: New York's automatic sealing of old criminal records
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted the Clean Slate Act, which automatically seals criminal records for people who have completed their sentences and waited a defined period without new offenses — three years for misdemeanors and eight years for felonies. This applies retroactively to hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers. Sealed records are not accessible to most employers or landlords, enabling people to find housing and employment without decades-old convictions following them. Records remain accessible for law enforcement, firearms purchases, and work in certain sensitive professions.
laws.penalty: Employers or landlords who discriminate based on improperly unsealed records face civil rights complaints; unauthorized access to sealed records by private parties carries fines
exceptions: Sex offenses subject to registration requirements are not eligible for sealing
Class A felonies (murder, rape at highest severity) cannot be sealed
Records sealed under Clean Slate remain visible for criminal background checks for law enforcement and sensitive positions

quiz.q: How long must a felony conviction be in the past before it is automatically sealed under New York's Clean Slate Act?
quiz.explanation: New York's Clean Slate Act automatically seals felony convictions after 8 years have passed since completion of sentence with no new offenses — three years for misdemeanors — enabling people to move on from old convictions in housing and employment.

laws.title: New York LLC Transparency Act
laws.subtitle: Requiring disclosure of beneficial owners of limited liability companies
laws.fullDescription: New York's LLC Transparency Act (signed 2023, phased implementation through 2026) requires limited liability companies registered or doing business in New York to disclose their true beneficial owners to the New York Department of State. The law was modeled on the federal Corporate Transparency Act and is designed to combat money laundering through anonymous shell companies in New York's real estate and business markets. The information is not publicly available but accessible to law enforcement.
laws.penalty: LLCs that fail to disclose beneficial owners or submit false information face civil penalties of $500 per day, up to a maximum of $10,000. Corporate officers who knowingly submit false information face criminal charges.
exceptions: Publicly traded companies and SEC-registered entities exempt from state filing (already subject to federal disclosure)
LLCs used exclusively by individual sole proprietors with no employees have simplified compliance path
Attorney-client privilege protects law firm operating accounts from ownership disclosure

quiz.q: What is the daily civil penalty for LLCs that fail to disclose beneficial owners under NY's LLC Transparency Act?
quiz.explanation: New York's LLC Transparency Act imposes civil penalties of $500 per day on LLCs that fail to disclose beneficial owners, capped at $10,000 total. The law targets anonymous shell companies used for money laundering in New York's real estate and business markets.

laws.title: New York Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) Implementation
laws.subtitle: State's landmark climate law mandating 70% renewable electricity by 2030
laws.fullDescription: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA, 2019) required 70% renewable electricity by 2030 and 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040. Implementation faced headwinds in 2022–2024 as offshore wind projects were cancelled or renegotiated due to supply chain inflation, rising interest rates, and contract pricing issues. Governor Hochul restructured offshore wind contract approvals, offered new pricing frameworks, and accelerated permitting for solar and battery storage to keep the 2030 target achievable.
laws.penalty: Utilities that fail to procure required renewable energy certificates (RECs) under their renewable portfolio standard obligations face penalties of $10 per MWh shortfall, paid to the NY Green Bank.
exceptions: Nuclear power plants qualify as carbon-free generation under the CLCPA's 100% target
Existing hydropower from Canadian imports counts toward renewable targets under bilateral agreements
Islands and remote communities not connected to the main grid may meet targets through island-appropriate renewables on different timelines

quiz.q: What percentage of renewable electricity does New York's CLCPA require by 2030?
quiz.explanation: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act requires 70% renewable electricity by 2030, with 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040. Implementation faced setbacks when offshore wind projects were cancelled due to inflation and rising costs, requiring New York to restructure its offshore wind contracting approach.

laws.title: New York City of Yes for Housing Opportunity
laws.subtitle: Largest zoning reform in NYC history
laws.fullDescription: New York City approved the 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' zoning reform in December 2024, the largest overhaul of NYC zoning rules in 60 years. Key changes include allowing small apartments above shops (universal affordability preference), ending parking minimums for most new housing, legalizing accessory dwelling units (ADUs), permitting office-to-residential conversions citywide, and allowing greater density near transit. The reform was projected to enable approximately 80,000 new housing units over 15 years.
laws.penalty: Construction of housing that violates the updated zoning regulations: stop-work orders and violations with fines under the NYC Administrative Code. Property owners who misrepresent conversion projects to access streamlined ADU permits: civil penalties.
exceptions: Historic districts retain restrictions on visible exterior changes regardless of zoning liberalization
Flood-prone zones have additional requirements before development permitted
Landmarks Commission review preserved for designated landmark buildings

quiz.q: How many new housing units did NYC's 'City of Yes' reform project to enable over 15 years?
quiz.explanation: NYC's 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' zoning reform was projected to enable approximately 80,000 new housing units over 15 years — described as the largest NYC zoning overhaul in 60 years, addressing the city's severe housing shortage through increased density, ADU legalization, and parking minimum elimination.

laws.title: Freelance Isn't Free Act Expansion
laws.subtitle: New York State expands freelancer payment protections statewide
laws.fullDescription: New York State expanded its Freelance Isn't Free Act — originally a New York City law — to protect all freelance workers throughout the state. The law requires written contracts for freelance work worth $800 or more, mandates payment within 30 days, and allows freelancers to sue for double damages plus attorney fees for non-payment. New York State became a national model for gig economy worker protections.
laws.penalty: Non-payment to freelancers: double damages plus attorney fees; failure to provide written contract: $250 penalty
exceptions: Sales commissions under separate commercial law provisions
Work by licensed attorneys under retainer agreements governed by bar rules

quiz.q: What financial penalty can freelancers in New York claim for non-payment?
quiz.explanation: New York's Freelance Isn't Free Act allows freelancers to sue for double damages (twice the unpaid amount) plus attorney fees when clients fail to pay within the required timeframe.

laws.title: New York Climate Corporate Accountability Act
laws.subtitle: NY requires large companies to disclose and pay for climate damages
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted the Climate Corporate Accountability Act (CCAA) requiring large companies with revenues over $1 billion doing business in New York to report Scope 1, 2, and 3 greenhouse gas emissions. The law went beyond California's climate disclosure law by including strict liability provisions and creating a state climate superfund that charges major fossil fuel companies proportionally for their historical emissions.
laws.penalty: Non-disclosure of required emissions data: fines up to $100,000 per day; fossil fuel companies: assessed contributions to climate superfund
exceptions: Small businesses under $1 billion revenue exempt from disclosure requirements
Non-profits and government agencies not covered by commercial reporting requirements

quiz.q: What makes New York's climate law go further than California's similar law?
options: It includes strict liability provisions and a fossil fuel climate superfund
quiz.explanation: New York's CCAA goes further than California's climate disclosure law by including strict liability provisions and creating a climate superfund that charges major fossil fuel companies proportionally for their historical greenhouse gas emissions.

laws.title: New York Public Utilities Clean Energy Standard
laws.subtitle: NY mandates 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040
laws.fullDescription: New York accelerated its Clean Energy Standard, requiring 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040 and all new building heating to be electric by 2030 in New York City and 2035 statewide. The Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) mandated that 35-40% of climate investments benefit disadvantaged communities. Offshore wind projects off Long Island were a key delivery mechanism.
laws.penalty: Utilities failing to meet renewable portfolio standards: fines per MWh of non-compliant electricity supplied
exceptions: Existing long-term power purchase contracts receive modified compliance timelines
Emergency reserve capacity not subject to zero-emission requirement during grid reliability events

quiz.q: What percentage of New York's climate investments must benefit disadvantaged communities under the CLCPA?
quiz.explanation: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) requires 35-40% of the benefits of climate investments to go to disadvantaged communities — one of the most ambitious environmental justice provisions in any US state climate law.

laws.title: New York Housing Compact and Zoning Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Mandating density near transit to address housing crisis
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted the Housing Compact and Transit-Oriented Development Act 2025 after years of housing affordability crisis in New York City and the broader metro region. The law requires municipalities within half a mile of commuter rail stations to permit residential development at minimum 50 units per acre density, removes parking minimums in transit-accessible areas, mandates that 20% of units in developments receiving state financing be permanently affordable, creates a state override for local zoning that fails to meet pro-housing targets, and establishes the New York Housing Accelerator to streamline environmental reviews for residential projects. Local governments that comply receive preferential state infrastructure funding.
laws.penalty: Local zoning ordinance blocking state-compliant housing applications: loss of state discretionary funding; discriminatory permit denial: $500,000 civil penalty plus private right of action; false affordability certification: 15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Historic districts retain modified density standards with design guidelines
Flood-vulnerable coastal zones exempt from minimum density requirements
Municipal home rule preserved for design standards not affecting allowable density
laws.sourceLabel: NY State Homes and Community Renewal

quiz.q: What minimum density does New York's Housing Compact require near commuter rail stations?
quiz.explanation: New York's Housing Compact requires municipalities within half a mile of commuter rail stations to permit residential development at a minimum density of 50 units per acre, aimed at creating walkable, transit-accessible housing near train stations.

laws.title: New York Climate Leadership and Community Protection Implementation
laws.subtitle: Enforcing the nation's most ambitious climate law
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) Full Implementation Act 2025, providing enforcement mechanisms and specific investment frameworks for its landmark 2019 law. The Act creates the Climate Action Council's binding sectoral emissions limits with compliance timelines and penalties, establishes the Climate Justice Working Group's Community Air Monitoring Network in 35 priority environmental justice communities, mandates that 40% of all climate investments benefit disadvantaged communities (increased from 35%), creates a Just Transition Fund with $10 billion for fossil fuel worker retraining, and establishes New York's first carbon border adjustment fee on electricity imports from states without comparable carbon pricing.
laws.penalty: Utility non-compliance with sectoral emission limits: $1 million per day; carbon border adjustment fee evasion: triple unpaid amount; disadvantaged community investment fraud: $50 million plus clawback
exceptions: Emergency grid reliability situations may trigger temporary compliance delays
Small utilities under 100,000 customers have extended compliance timelines
Research and academic electric consumption has modified framework

quiz.q: What percentage of New York's climate investments must benefit disadvantaged communities under the 2025 CLCPA Implementation Act?
quiz.explanation: New York's CLCPA Full Implementation Act increased the requirement that climate investments benefit disadvantaged communities from 35% to 40% — a significant commitment ensuring environmental justice communities receive direct benefits from the state's climate spending.

laws.title: New York Congestion Pricing Defense and MTA Funding Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting and expanding first US congestion pricing
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted the Congestion Pricing Defense and Metropolitan Transportation Authority Funding Act 2025, protecting the landmark congestion pricing programme that Governor Hochul had controversially paused in 2024 before restoring it under legal and political pressure. The law creates permanent legal protections for congestion pricing preventing unilateral gubernatorial suspension, establishes the Central Business District Toll Authority as independent entity (separate from MTA), mandates that 100% of collected revenues fund MTA capital projects, creates a hardship exemption programme for low-income drivers with $1,500 annual rebates, expands the programme to cover HOV violations and commercial delivery surcharges, and establishes performance metrics requiring MTA to demonstrate transit improvements linked to congestion pricing revenues.
laws.penalty: Toll evasion: $200 per violation plus $100 per day unpaid; unauthorized congestion pricing suspension: $1 billion fund withholding trigger; revenue diversion from MTA: criminal prosecution of responsible officials
exceptions: Emergency vehicles exempt from congestion pricing
Qualifying low-income residents with rebate program enrolled pay reduced tolls
Overnight hours (9pm-5am) have reduced rate pricing

quiz.q: What governor controversially paused New York's congestion pricing program in 2024, prompting the 2025 Defense Act?
quiz.explanation: Governor Kathy Hochul controversially paused New York's congestion pricing program in June 2024 just weeks before it was set to launch — citing economic concerns — before ultimately restoring it under political and legal pressure, prompting the 2025 Act to prevent future suspensions.

laws.title: Good Cause Eviction and Tenant Protection Expansion Act
laws.subtitle: Expanding renter rights across New York State
laws.fullDescription: New York State enacted sweeping tenant protection legislation extending good cause eviction protections statewide. The law requires landlords to provide documented just cause for evictions, caps rent increases at the lower of 3% or 1.5 times the Consumer Price Index, creates a right to lease renewal, and establishes a state tenant protection fund to support tenants facing eviction. The legislation builds on the landmark 2019 Housing Stability Act.
laws.penalty: Landlords who evict tenants without cause face civil penalties up to $15,000 and are liable for tenant relocation costs. Rent overcharges carry treble damages plus attorney fees.
exceptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units are exempt
New construction is exempt for the first 30 years from certificate of occupancy

quiz.q: What formula does New York's Good Cause Eviction law use to cap annual rent increases?
options: 3% or 1.5 times CPI, whichever is lower
quiz.explanation: New York's Good Cause law caps rent increases at the lower of 3% or 1.5 times the Consumer Price Index, protecting tenants from large rent hikes while allowing landlords modest annual increases.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing Implementation and Transit Reinvestment Act
laws.subtitle: First US congestion toll zone funds MTA improvements
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted legislation fully implementing Manhattan's congestion pricing zone — the first in the United States — after years of legal and political delays. The law establishes the toll structure for vehicles entering Manhattan below 60th Street, dedicates all revenue exclusively to the MTA capital program, creates exemptions and credits for qualifying vehicles, and establishes a board to adjust toll rates based on traffic conditions.
laws.penalty: Vehicles that evade tolls through removed or obscured license plates face fines up to $1,000 per violation. License plate obscuring devices carry additional criminal charges.
exceptions: Certified low-income drivers who regularly commute into the zone receive partial toll credits
Vehicles transporting people with disabilities who cannot use public transportation receive exemptions

quiz.q: What is notable about New York City's congestion pricing zone in the context of the United States?
options: It is the largest toll road in America
It is the first congestion pricing zone in the US
It was approved unanimously by Congress
It applies to all five boroughs
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing zone in lower Manhattan is the first of its kind in the United States. Similar programs have been operating in London, Stockholm, and Singapore for years.

laws.title: Hudson River Restoration and Climate Resilience Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting waterway from sea level rise and pollution
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted comprehensive Hudson River protection legislation, building on decades of environmental cleanup since the river's industrial pollution era. The law creates new sea level rise protections for Hudson River communities, establishes a Hudson River Estuary Climate Resilience Program, restricts new industrial discharges that reversed progress on PCB cleanup, creates public waterfront access requirements, and funds nature-based flood barriers.
laws.penalty: Industrial facilities that discharge above permitted levels into the Hudson face fines up to $37,500 per day per violation. Development that blocks public waterfront access in violation of the public trust doctrine faces removal orders.
exceptions: Working waterfronts serving maritime and fishing industries retain operational access even where public access is mandated
Agricultural operations that have pre-Clean Water Act permits retain modified discharge allowances

quiz.q: What toxic chemical contaminated the Hudson River for decades following industrial dumping by General Electric?
quiz.explanation: General Electric dumped PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) into the Hudson River from its capacitor plants for decades. PCBs are persistent toxic chemicals that bioaccumulate in fish, triggering long-term fishing advisories and a massive (and controversial) dredging cleanup.

laws.title: New York Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act
laws.subtitle: Anti-Displacement and Community Land Trust Law
laws.fullDescription: Gives tenants and community organizations the right of first refusal to purchase residential buildings when landlords decide to sell. The law creates a 180-day window for tenant associations or nonprofits to match any sale offer, establishes below-market financing through a state land trust fund, and requires building inspections before sales to ensure habitability. The law aims to combat displacement in New York's housing crisis.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $500,000 for landlords who violate tenant purchase rights; void of non-compliant sales
exceptions: Owner-occupied buildings with up to 3 units
Buildings sold to immediate family members

quiz.q: How long do New York tenants have to exercise their purchase right under TOPA?
quiz.explanation: New York's Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act gives tenants a 180-day window to match any sale offer on their building.

laws.title: New York Grieving Families Act and Wrongful Death Reform
laws.subtitle: Expanded Damages and Survivor Rights Law
laws.fullDescription: Expands New York's wrongful death statute to allow recovery for grief and emotional suffering by surviving family members, bringing New York in line with most states. The law allows parents, siblings, and domestic partners to recover non-economic damages, extends the statute of limitations from 2 to 3.5 years, and eliminates the provision that limited recovery to economic damages only. The old law was often criticized for creating perverse incentives in wrongful death cases.
laws.penalty: Extended damages available to families in wrongful death litigation; court-ordered non-economic damages
exceptions: Government immunity protections remain in force
Medical malpractice cases follow separate statutory framework

quiz.q: What new type of damages does New York's Grieving Families Act allow in wrongful death cases?
options: Pain and suffering for the deceased
quiz.explanation: New York's Grieving Families Act allows surviving family members to recover damages for grief and emotional suffering for the first time.

laws.title: New York Clean Slate Act and Criminal Record Sealing Law
laws.subtitle: Second Chance Employment and Record Sealing Reform
laws.fullDescription: Automatically seals criminal records after specified waiting periods: 3 years for misdemeanors and 8 years for most felonies. The law applies to individuals who have completed their sentences without new convictions, allows sealed records to be accessed only by law enforcement and courts, creates employment and housing protections for sealed record holders, and does not apply to sex offenses or Class A felonies.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties for employers illegally accessing sealed records; discrimination claims for housing and employment
exceptions: Sex offenses permanently excluded from sealing
Class A felonies including murder excluded
Records accessible to law enforcement for investigations

quiz.q: How long must someone wait after a felony conviction for New York's Clean Slate Act to automatically seal their record?
quiz.explanation: New York's Clean Slate Act automatically seals most felony convictions after 8 years of completing sentences without new convictions.

laws.title: New York Responsible and Equitable Regulation of Cannabis Act
laws.subtitle: Cannabis Dispensary Licensing and Equity Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements New York's cannabis retail licensing program years after legalization, addressing licensing delays that allowed illicit shops to proliferate. The law creates social equity licenses prioritizing those convicted of cannabis offenses, establishes the Cannabis Control Board's enforcement against unlicensed shops, creates the New York Cannabis Hub for social equity operators, and establishes quality control testing requirements.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $25,000 per day for unlicensed cannabis retail operations; law enforcement shutdown authority
exceptions: Medical cannabis dispensaries continue under separate license
Home cultivation of up to 6 plants for personal use remains legal

quiz.q: What problem plagued New York's cannabis market during licensing delays?
quiz.explanation: New York's slow rollout of licensed cannabis dispensaries allowed thousands of illicit unlicensed shops to proliferate, undermining the legal market.

laws.title: Good Cause Eviction Statewide Expansion
laws.subtitle: Tenant Protection Law Limits No-Fault Evictions
laws.fullDescription: New York expanded good cause eviction protections statewide, limiting landlords' ability to evict tenants without a legitimate reason and capping allowable rent increases. The law significantly shifted tenant-landlord balance in a state with severe housing affordability challenges.
laws.penalty: Evictions without good cause prohibited; landlords liable for damages
exceptions: Buildings with fewer than 4 units where landlord lives
Buildings constructed in last 30 years

quiz.q: What does New York's Good Cause Eviction law primarily restrict?
options: No-fault evictions and excessive rent increases
quiz.explanation: New York's Good Cause Eviction law restricts landlords from evicting tenants without cause and caps allowable rent increases.

laws.title: Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
laws.subtitle: NY Implements 70% Renewable Energy by 2030
laws.fullDescription: New York began full implementation of the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, one of the most ambitious US state climate laws. The law required 70% renewable electricity by 2030 and 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040. Implementation faced challenges including offshore wind project cancellations due to inflation and supply chain issues.
laws.penalty: Agency compliance requirements; penalties for failing to meet procurement goals
exceptions: Reliability emergency provisions
Federal grid interconnection constraints

quiz.q: What does New York's CLCPA require by 2030?
quiz.explanation: New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act requires 70% renewable electricity by 2030 and 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040.

laws.title: Executive Order on AI in State Government
laws.subtitle: New York Regulates AI Use in Public Sector
laws.fullDescription: New York issued a comprehensive executive order and followed with legislation governing the use of artificial intelligence in state government, requiring impact assessments, bias audits, and transparency for high-risk AI systems used in benefits, housing, employment, and criminal justice decisions.
laws.penalty: State agency compliance required; civil rights enforcement for bias
exceptions: Research and pilot programs
Emergency exception provisions

quiz.q: In what government areas does New York require AI bias audits?
options: Benefits, housing, employment, and criminal justice
quiz.explanation: New York requires AI impact assessments and bias audits for high-risk AI systems used in benefits, housing, employment, and criminal justice decisions.

laws.title: Trump Criminal Trial and Presidential Immunity
laws.subtitle: New York Convicts Former President on Hush Money Charges
laws.fullDescription: Former President Donald Trump was convicted in May 2024 on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to hush money payments, becoming the first US president convicted of criminal charges. The case involved payments to Stormy Daniels before the 2016 election. Trump was sentenced but faced no jail time.
