laws.penalty: Guilty verdict on 34 counts; sentenced to unconditional discharge
exceptions: Presidential immunity Supreme Court ruling for official acts
Sentencing considerations for former president

quiz.q: What historic first did Donald Trump achieve with the New York criminal trial?
options: First former US president convicted of criminal charges
First president tried in state court
quiz.explanation: Donald Trump became the first former US president to be convicted of criminal charges when a New York jury found him guilty on 34 felony counts in May 2024.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing and Green Transportation
laws.subtitle: NYC Implements Nation's First Congestion Toll
laws.fullDescription: New York City implemented the nation's first congestion pricing system in 2024, charging drivers $9 for vehicles entering Manhattan below 60th Street. The revenue funded subway and bus improvements. The program aimed to reduce congestion and shift commuters to transit. Federal opposition under the Trump administration created legal battles.
laws.penalty: $9-23 tolls depending on vehicle type; violations subject to fines
exceptions: Emergency vehicles exempt
Disability exemptions
Residents under income threshold rebate

quiz.q: What is New York City's congestion pricing toll for most vehicles?
quiz.explanation: New York City charges $9 for most passenger vehicles entering Manhattan below 60th Street under the nation's first congestion pricing system.

laws.title: Climate Superfund Law and Fossil Fuel Company Liability
laws.subtitle: New York makes oil companies pay for climate damages
laws.fullDescription: New York passed the Climate Change Superfund Act, requiring the largest fossil fuel companies to pay $75 billion toward climate adaptation costs based on their historical emissions contributions. The law, modeled after the federal Superfund for toxic waste, is the first of its kind and is being challenged by oil companies as unconstitutional. If upheld, it could transform climate litigation and provide a model for other states. The funds would pay for seawall construction, infrastructure upgrades, and flood protection.
laws.penalty: Major fossil fuel companies must pay into the climate superfund based on their proportional historical emissions
exceptions: Small producers below threshold size exempt from superfund contributions
Companies that have undergone bankruptcy restructuring may have limited liability

quiz.q: How much must fossil fuel companies pay under New York's Climate Superfund Act?
quiz.explanation: New York's Climate Superfund Act requires major fossil fuel companies to collectively pay $75 billion toward climate adaptation costs, proportional to their historical emissions contributions.

laws.title: Crypto Regulation and BitLicense Expansion
laws.subtitle: New York maintains strict cryptocurrency oversight as industry grows
laws.fullDescription: New York's BitLicense, created in 2015, remains the world's strictest cryptocurrency regulatory framework. Getting a BitLicense costs millions and takes years. Critics say it drove crypto businesses to other states. Proponents say it protects consumers. New York updated its framework to cover DeFi and stablecoins. After the FTX collapse, New York's stringent approach looks prescient. The state is also developing blockchain-based land records and other government applications.
laws.penalty: Operating a cryptocurrency business in New York without a BitLicense or exemption carries criminal and civil penalties
exceptions: Non-custodial wallets where users control their own keys have different regulatory treatment
Merchant acceptance of crypto payments has lighter requirements than exchange operations

laws.title: Housing Supply Crisis and Zoning Reform Battle
laws.subtitle: New York State attempts to override NIMBYist suburban zoning
laws.fullDescription: New York State faces a catastrophic housing shortage, especially in the New York City metropolitan area. Governor Hochul proposed ambitious zoning reforms requiring municipalities to allow more housing — especially near transit — but faced fierce resistance from wealthy suburbs. The legislature watered down or blocked major reforms. New York City has been rezoning areas for more density. The housing crisis drives workers out of the region. NYC's housing cost is among the highest globally, consuming enormous shares of residents' incomes.
laws.penalty: New York City limits on rent stabilized apartments constrain how much landlords can raise rents
exceptions: New construction receives 421-a tax exemption for affordable housing inclusion
Owner-occupied buildings under certain unit thresholds exempt from rent stabilization

quiz.q: What obstacle blocked New York's ambitious housing reform attempts?
options: State legislature blocking it after fierce resistance from wealthy suburbs
quiz.explanation: New York's housing reform attempts were blocked by fierce resistance from wealthy suburban municipalities that oppose density — with the state legislature bending to NIMBY pressure rather than allowing Governor Hochul's plans.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing Reversal and Transit Funding Crisis
laws.subtitle: New York's landmark traffic pricing scheme and its political fate
laws.fullDescription: New York City's congestion pricing program — the first in the United States — was designed to charge vehicles entering Manhattan south of 60th Street, using revenues to fund subway and bus improvements. The $15 base toll for passenger cars was approved after years of debate and was expected to generate $1 billion annually for the MTA. However, Governor Kathy Hochul paused the program in June 2024, citing economic concerns about businesses and transit riders, just weeks before it was set to launch. The pause prompted legal challenges from the MTA, transit advocates, and environmental groups, arguing the governor lacked authority to override the program. New York's subway, bus, and commuter rail systems face a significant funding gap for capital improvements. The congestion pricing battle illustrates tensions between urban mobility goals, economic concerns, and political calculations.
laws.penalty: Congestion pricing violations (when active) carry fines similar to tolling violations; MTA fare evasion carries civil penalties
exceptions: Emergency vehicles, certain disabled persons, and some low-income commuters were to receive exemptions or credits

quiz.q: What made New York City's congestion pricing program historically significant?
options: It was the largest toll in US history
It was the first congestion pricing program in the United States
It generated the most revenue of any urban toll program
It covered the largest geographic area of any pricing zone
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing program was the first in the United States, designed to charge vehicles entering lower Manhattan to reduce traffic and fund transit improvements, though it was controversially paused before implementation.

laws.title: Crypto Regulation and BitLicense Framework
laws.subtitle: New York's strict cryptocurrency regulatory approach
laws.fullDescription: New York State established one of the world's most comprehensive cryptocurrency regulatory frameworks through its BitLicense system, launched in 2015. The BitLicense requires companies conducting virtual currency business activities with New York residents to obtain a license from the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), meeting requirements for consumer protection, cybersecurity, anti-money laundering, and capital reserves. The strict requirements led many crypto companies to initially avoid New York entirely (the New York Exemption), but as the industry matured, major firms sought licenses. The collapse of FTX in 2022 and subsequent crypto industry failures reinforced New York's regulatory approach. Gemini, regulated by NYDFS, was one of the survivors of the crypto winter. New York has also been active in prosecuting crypto fraud and Ponzi schemes.
laws.penalty: Operating without a BitLicense carries criminal and civil penalties including fines and possible imprisonment for principals
exceptions: Some activities involving virtual currency fall below licensing thresholds or within exemptions for merchant activities

quiz.q: What is the BitLicense system New York established in 2015?
options: A comprehensive licensing framework for companies conducting cryptocurrency business with NY residents
A blockchain certification for financial institutions
quiz.explanation: New York's BitLicense, launched in 2015, requires companies conducting virtual currency business activities with New York residents to meet strict licensing requirements covering consumer protection, cybersecurity, anti-money laundering, and capital reserves.

laws.title: Wall Street AI and Algorithmic Trading Regulation
laws.subtitle: New York financial regulators grappling with AI in markets
laws.fullDescription: New York State and the SEC have been developing frameworks to address artificial intelligence in financial markets — from AI-powered trading algorithms to AI-generated investment advice to deepfake market manipulation risks. Algorithmic trading already accounts for the majority of US equity market volume, creating both efficiency gains and flash crash risks. High-frequency trading firms based in and around New York use AI to execute trades in microseconds. New York's Department of Financial Services has issued guidance on AI use by regulated institutions, requiring governance frameworks, explainability, and bias testing for AI in credit decisions. The SEC has proposed rules on predictive data analytics by investment advisers. New York's position as a global financial center means its regulatory approach influences global standards for AI in finance.
laws.penalty: SEC and FINRA violations carry fines and potential criminal prosecution; DFS violations affect state licensing
exceptions: Academic research and certain non-commercial algorithmic activities may have different regulatory treatment

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of US equity market volume does algorithmic trading account for?
quiz.explanation: Algorithmic trading accounts for the majority of US equity market volume — creating efficiency gains but also systemic risks like flash crashes that concern regulators developing AI oversight frameworks.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing Launch and Rollback Drama
laws.subtitle: Manhattan tolling program implemented then paused then restored
laws.fullDescription: New York City launched the nation's first congestion pricing program in June 2024, charging drivers entering Manhattan below 60th Street. Governor Kathy Hochul paused the program just weeks later, citing economic concerns, triggering a legal battle with the MTA and transit advocates. A court ordered the program restored. The on-again-off-again saga highlighted political tensions between transit funding needs and driver constituencies. When fully operational, congestion pricing aimed to raise billions for subway improvements.
laws.penalty: Violations of toll payment requirements subject to fines; unpaid tolls accumulate and can trigger registration holds
exceptions: Vehicles with disability placards receive exemptions
Emergency vehicles and certain government vehicles exempt

quiz.q: New York's congestion pricing program charges drivers entering Manhattan below what street?
quiz.explanation: New York's congestion pricing program charges drivers entering the Congestion Relief Zone, which covers Manhattan below 60th Street, making it the first such program in the United States.

laws.title: AI Hiring Bias Audit Law
laws.subtitle: New York City requires bias audits for AI hiring tools
laws.fullDescription: New York City enacted Local Law 144, requiring employers using automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) to conduct annual bias audits and notify job applicants when such tools are used. The law was the first in the US to regulate AI in hiring decisions with teeth. Compliance has been inconsistent and the audit industry has faced criticism for shallow compliance over genuine bias detection. The law created a model that other jurisdictions have considered adopting.
laws.penalty: Violations of bias audit requirement subject to civil penalties of up to $1,500 per violation per day
exceptions: Tools that only assess seniority or tenure exempt
Human resource tools with no automated component not covered

quiz.q: What does New York City's Local Law 144 require employers to do with AI hiring tools?
options: Conduct annual bias audits and notify applicants
quiz.explanation: NYC Local Law 144 requires employers to conduct annual bias audits of automated employment decision tools and notify job applicants when such tools are used—the first US law with enforcement teeth on AI hiring bias.

laws.title: Housing Supply Crisis and Zoning Reform
laws.subtitle: New York struggles to build enough homes for its population
laws.fullDescription: New York City has a severe housing shortage with vacancy rates among the lowest of any major city. The state has passed legislation requiring localities to meet housing production targets, overriding restrictive local zoning. The Adams administration pushed for housing supply increases including office-to-residential conversions. The City of Yes planning reform approved in late 2024 was the most significant zoning update in decades. New York's housing crisis drives inequality and worker displacement to other regions.
laws.penalty: Localities failing housing production targets can be overridden by state; office conversions receive tax incentives
exceptions: Historic districts have modified requirements
Affordable housing income restrictions remain even with zoning liberalization

quiz.q: What was the name of New York City's major 2024 zoning reform initiative?
quiz.explanation: City of Yes was approved in late 2024 as the most significant zoning update in New York City in decades, allowing more housing construction across the city to address the severe housing shortage that keeps vacancy rates near historic lows.

laws.title: Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Most Ambitious US State Climate Law
laws.fullDescription: New York's CLCPA, signed in 2019, sets the most aggressive climate targets of any US state: 70% renewable electricity by 2030, 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040, and economy-wide net zero emissions by 2050. The law also mandates that 35-40% of climate investments benefit disadvantaged communities that have historically borne the burden of pollution, creating an environmental justice framework tied directly to climate policy.
laws.penalty: Regulatory enforcement by DEC; projects failing to comply with offsets face permit denial
exceptions: Emergency backup power systems
Critical infrastructure with no viable alternatives

laws.title: New York City Lead Paint Law
laws.subtitle: Protecting Children from Lead Poisoning
laws.fullDescription: New York City's Local Law 1 (2004) is considered the nation's strongest lead paint law, requiring building owners to proactively inspect and remediate lead paint hazards in apartments where children under 6 live. NYC has dramatically reduced childhood lead poisoning rates — from 20,000+ children with elevated blood lead levels in the 1970s to under 1,000 today. The law requires annual visual inspections and immediate remediation of peeling or chipping lead paint. NYC also prohibits abrasive methods that spread lead dust without containment.
laws.penalty: Fines from $250 to $10,000+ for violations; stop-work orders; criminal liability for willful violations
exceptions: Owner-occupied one and two-family homes (reduced requirements)
Buildings with no children under 6

laws.title: New York Fast Food Worker Protections
laws.subtitle: Scheduling Rights and Minimum Wages
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted landmark fast food worker protections: minimum wage for fast food workers rising to $17/hour (above the state minimum); just-cause termination protection (cannot be fired without cause from major chains); and predictive scheduling laws requiring advance notice of schedules. New York's HERO Act also requires employers to develop airborne infectious disease exposure plans. The 'just cause' protection for fast food workers — passed in 2021 — was the first in the US, preventing chains from firing workers without documented valid reason.
laws.penalty: Just-cause violations: reinstatement plus back pay; scheduling violations: premium pay per shift; wage theft: treble damages
exceptions: Just-cause protection applies to chains with 100+ locations nationally
Small restaurants and franchises under different thresholds

laws.title: New York Excelsior Scholarship
laws.subtitle: Free Tuition for Middle-Class Families
laws.fullDescription: New York's Excelsior Scholarship (2017) provides free tuition at SUNY and CUNY colleges for students from families earning under $125,000/year, covering costs not met by other financial aid. This was the first state program in the US to offer free tuition at public universities. New York also has the Tuition Assistance Program (TAP) for lower-income students. New York City's public school system — the nation's largest — spends over $30,000 per pupil per year. New York has strong teacher union representation (UFT — United Federation of Teachers) and comprehensive bilingual education programs for its large immigrant population.
laws.penalty: Scholarship recipients must work in New York State for the same number of years as scholarship received, or repay funds
exceptions: Students attending private colleges ineligible
Part-time students must be full-time to qualify

laws.title: Driver's License Access and Privacy Act
laws.subtitle: New York's 'Green Light Law' for undocumented immigrants
laws.fullDescription: New York's Driver's License Access and Privacy Act (2019), known as the 'Green Light Law,' allows all New York residents to obtain standard driver's licenses regardless of immigration status. The law also restricts DMV from sharing license holder data with federal immigration authorities unless presented with a judicial warrant. New York joined a dozen states offering licenses to undocumented residents. The law faced legal challenges from the Trump administration and several upstate counties but was upheld. Approximately 750,000 undocumented immigrants in New York can now legally drive.
laws.penalty: DMV employees sharing license data with federal immigration authorities without warrant face disciplinary action; ICE cannot access DMV records without judicial warrant under state law
exceptions: REAL ID-compliant licenses (for federal purposes like airport security) still require proof of legal status
Drivers must pass same road tests and insurance requirements as any license applicant
laws.sourceLabel: New York Green Light Law (Vehicle & Traffic Law §502)

quiz.q: New York's 'Green Light Law' allows undocumented residents to obtain what?
quiz.explanation: New York's Green Light Law (2019) allows all state residents regardless of immigration status to obtain standard state driver's licenses (not REAL ID-compliant federal IDs), enabling legal driving and access to car insurance.

laws.title: Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act
laws.subtitle: New York's cannabis legalization and social equity
laws.fullDescription: New York's MRTA (2021) legalized recreational cannabis with a strong social equity focus: 50% of cannabis business licenses reserved for 'social and economic equity' applicants (individuals from communities disproportionately impacted by cannabis criminalization). The Office of Cannabis Management (OCM) launched the Conditional Adult Use Retail Dispensary (CAURD) program. New York faced implementation delays, with illegal dispensaries outnumbering licensed ones for years. The MRTA also automatically expunged records for prior cannabis convictions.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed retail sales: Class A misdemeanor to felony depending on quantity; cannabis use in prohibited areas: up to $25 fine; selling to minors: felony
exceptions: Adults 21+ may possess up to 3 oz cannabis and 24g concentrate
Home cultivation (up to 6 plants, 3 mature) permitted
Prior cannabis convictions automatically expunged under MRTA
laws.sourceLabel: New York Office of Cannabis Management (MRTA 2021)

quiz.q: New York's MRTA cannabis law reserved 50% of business licenses for what specific group?
options: Social equity applicants from communities harmed by drug enforcement
quiz.explanation: New York reserved 50% of cannabis retail licenses for 'social and economic equity' applicants — people with prior cannabis convictions, residents of high-enforcement communities, minority-owned businesses — in a deliberate attempt to direct cannabis wealth to communities most harmed by the War on Drugs.

laws.title: Sexual Orientation Non-Discrimination Act
laws.subtitle: New York's LGBTQ+ protections and historic Stonewall
laws.fullDescription: New York City is home to the Stonewall Inn — site of the 1969 Stonewall Riots, the watershed moment of the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. New York State enacted the Sexual Orientation Non-Discrimination Act (SONDA) in 2002, adding sexual orientation to the state human rights law. New York legalized same-sex marriage in 2011 (Marriage Equality Act). The Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act (GENDA, 2019) added gender identity and expression. New York City has had domestic partnership registration since 1993 and comprehensive protections since the 1980s.
laws.penalty: Sexual orientation/gender identity discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation: civil liability up to $100,000 compensatory damages plus punitive damages; LGBTQ+ hate crimes: enhanced criminal penalties; conversion therapy on minors: license revocation for therapists
exceptions: Religious organizations retain some employment exemptions for coreligionist requirements
Small landlords (fewer than 4 units, owner-occupied) have limited fair housing exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: New York State Division of Human Rights LGBTQ+

quiz.q: The 1969 Stonewall Riots, widely credited as launching the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement, occurred at a bar in which New York City neighborhood?
quiz.explanation: The Stonewall Inn, location of the 1969 riots, is in Greenwich Village, Manhattan. The riots were a series of spontaneous protests by LGBTQ+ people against a police raid in the early hours of June 28, 1969. The Stonewall Inn is now a National Monument.

laws.title: Free Press Capital — New York Shield Law and Press Protections
laws.subtitle: New York has strong shield laws and is home to the nation's most influential press
laws.fullDescription: New York's Civil Rights Law Section 79-h provides strong shield protection for journalists against compelled disclosure of sources or unpublished information. New York City is home to the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Associated Press, and major broadcast networks. The state has strong anti-SLAPP laws (Citizen Participation Act) protecting journalists from frivolous lawsuits intended to silence reporting. New York courts have also applied First Amendment protections broadly. The state's Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) provides public access to government records.
laws.penalty: Journalists are protected from source disclosure; SLAPP suits can result in fee awards against plaintiffs
exceptions: Federal subpoenas and national security cases may override state protections

quiz.q: What is the purpose of New York's anti-SLAPP law (Citizen Participation Act) in relation to press freedom?
options: Prevent journalists from publishing without sources
Protect journalists from frivolous lawsuits meant to silence reporting
quiz.explanation: New York's anti-SLAPP law (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) protects journalists and others from frivolous lawsuits filed to silence reporting and public discourse, allowing courts to dismiss such suits and award fees.

laws.title: SAFE for Kids Act and Algorithmic Feed Restrictions
laws.subtitle: New York passed laws restricting addictive social media features for minors
laws.fullDescription: New York passed the Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act (2024), requiring social media platforms to obtain parental consent before showing minors algorithmically curated 'addictive feeds,' and requiring default chronological feeds for minors under 18. New York also passed the Child Data Protection Act limiting data collection on minors. These laws were challenged in federal court on First Amendment grounds. New York Attorney General has also investigated social media platforms for algorithmic harms. The laws reflect growing legislative concern about social media's mental health impact on young people.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties for violations of the SAFE for Kids Act; AG enforcement authority
exceptions: First Amendment challenges are ongoing in federal courts

quiz.q: What does New York's SAFE for Kids Act require regarding social media feeds for minors?
options: Ban minors from all social media
Parental consent for algorithmically curated addictive feeds and default chronological feeds
quiz.explanation: New York's SAFE for Kids Act requires social media platforms to obtain parental consent before showing minors algorithmically curated 'addictive feeds,' and mandates that minors receive chronological feeds by default — targeting the algorithm-driven content that research links to mental health harms.

laws.title: BitLicense and NY Financial Regulation — Global Banking Hub
laws.subtitle: New York's BitLicense is the world's first and most influential crypto regulatory framework
laws.fullDescription: New York is the world's most important banking center, home to JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and the New York Stock Exchange. The New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) is one of the most powerful state financial regulators globally. New York created the BitLicense in 2015 — the world's first comprehensive state cryptocurrency business license — requiring any business dealing in Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies in New York to apply for a license. NYDFS has fined major crypto firms billions and set a global regulatory precedent. New York's banking laws set industry standards nationally.
laws.penalty: BitLicense violations: fines up to $2 billion (Binance paid); NYDFS can revoke banking charters
exceptions: National banks are federally chartered but NYDFS retains consumer protection authority
laws.sourceLabel: New York Department of Financial Services

quiz.q: What was the BitLicense and why was it historically significant?
options: A Bitcoin tax in New York
The world's first state cryptocurrency business license (2015)
A federal banking exemption for crypto
quiz.explanation: New York's BitLicense (2015) was the world's first comprehensive state-level cryptocurrency business license, requiring any company dealing in Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies in New York to apply — setting a global regulatory precedent that influenced how other jurisdictions approached crypto regulation.

laws.title: NYC Restaurant Letter Grading & Trans Fat Ban
laws.subtitle: New York City pioneered mandatory restaurant letter grades and trans fat elimination
laws.fullDescription: New York City pioneered mandatory restaurant health inspection letter grades (A, B, C) displayed in windows, launching in 2010. The system transformed food safety compliance — restaurants with grade A achieve a target score of 0-13 points in inspections. NYC also pioneered the US trans fat ban (2006-2007), eliminating artificial trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) from restaurants years before the FDA acted nationally. New York State's Department of Agriculture and Markets regulates food manufacturing and distribution statewide, with detailed rules on temperature control, labeling, and food handler certification. NYC's Department of Health conducts unannounced restaurant inspections.
laws.penalty: Restaurant grade violations: fines based on point scoring ($200-$2,000 per violation); operating without grade display: $1,000 fine; trans fat violations when active: up to $2,000 per violation
exceptions: Religious food preparation for private consumption is exempt from many commercial rules
Home food businesses under cottage food laws have modified requirements
Temporary events with 30-day permits have modified inspection protocols

quiz.q: What pioneering food policy did New York City implement in 2006-2007 that the FDA didn't mandate nationally until later?
options: Mandatory A/B/C grade letter display for restaurants
Elimination of artificial trans fats from restaurant food
Banning plastic packaging for food service
quiz.explanation: NYC banned artificial trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) from restaurants in 2006-2007, years ahead of the FDA's national ban. The city also led on mandatory calorie labeling, which it implemented before federal requirements.

laws.title: New York Companion Animal Care and Anti-Cruelty Laws
laws.subtitle: NY bans cat declawing and mandates shelter standards
laws.fullDescription: New York enacted significant animal welfare protections including the first US state ban on cat declawing (onychectomy) in 2019 — the procedure is now a misdemeanor for veterinarians performing elective declaws. The NY Agriculture & Markets Law Article 26 governs animal cruelty — felony charges apply for aggravated cruelty. New York City's CACC shelter system must meet minimum care standards. The ANIMAL Act expanded protections for farm animals. New York also bans the sale of dogs and cats in pet stores unless sourced from rescues, mirroring California.
laws.penalty: Misdemeanor animal cruelty: up to 1 year; felony aggravated cruelty: up to 2 years; cat declaw violation: up to $1,000 fine per procedure
exceptions: Therapeutic declaw for medical conditions affecting cat's health remains legal
Livestock operations under Department of Agriculture oversight
Research animals covered under federal Animal Welfare Act

quiz.q: What made New York a landmark state in animal welfare in 2019?
options: First US state to ban cat declawing
First to grant animals legal personhood
quiz.explanation: In 2019, New York became the first US state to ban cat declawing (onychectomy) as an elective procedure, making it a misdemeanor for veterinarians to perform the surgery for non-therapeutic reasons.

laws.title: New York Divorce Law and Equitable Distribution
laws.subtitle: New York was the last US state to adopt no-fault divorce in 2010
laws.fullDescription: New York was the last US state to adopt no-fault divorce — enacted in 2010, making it the 50th state to do so. Prior to 2010, New York required proving fault (abandonment, cruelty, adultery) to divorce. New York is an equitable distribution state (not community property) — courts divide marital assets fairly but not necessarily equally, considering factors like marriage length, each spouse's economic circumstances, and contributions. New York recognizes domestic violence orders of protection through Family Court. Child support follows the Income Shares Model formula. Alimony (maintenance) is determined by formula with judicial discretion. New York City family courts handle high volumes with long wait times.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; contempt of court for violating family court orders: fines and imprisonment; child support non-payment: licence suspension, wage garnishment, credit reporting
exceptions: Premarital agreements (prenups) can override equitable distribution
Separate property retains individual ownership
Gifts and inheritance remain separate

quiz.q: What made New York unusual among US states regarding divorce law until 2010?
options: New York banned remarriage after divorce
New York was the last US state to adopt no-fault divorce — requiring fault proof until 2010
New York required court approval for all marriages
New York didn't recognize divorce at all
quiz.explanation: New York was the last of all 50 US states to adopt no-fault divorce, finally doing so in 2010. Until then, New York required proving fault grounds (cruelty, abandonment, adultery) for divorce — a major obstacle that pushed many couples to establish short-term residency in other states to divorce there.

laws.title: New York Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Landmark 2019 rent regulation overhaul
laws.fullDescription: The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 fundamentally reformed New York's rent regulation system. It eliminated 'vacancy decontrol' (which allowed landlords to deregulate apartments when rents hit thresholds), made rent stabilization permanent, limited rent increases for Individual Apartment Improvements (IAIs), and strengthened protections against harassment and wrongful eviction. Over one million apartments remain under rent stabilization in New York City.
laws.penalty: Landlords face treble damages for overcharging rent; harassment carries civil penalties up to $15,000 per violation
exceptions: Luxury deregulation eliminated
High-income deregulation eliminated
laws.sourceLabel: NY Housing Stability & Tenant Protection Act 2019

quiz.q: What did the 2019 NY HSTPA eliminate that previously allowed landlords to deregulate apartments?
quiz.explanation: The HSTPA eliminated 'vacancy decontrol,' which had previously allowed landlords to remove apartments from rent stabilization when rents hit a threshold upon vacancy, ending a major loophole.

laws.title: New York SHIELD Act & Consumer Protection Laws
laws.subtitle: Data security and broad consumer protection enforcement
laws.fullDescription: New York's Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security (SHIELD) Act (2019) expanded the definition of private information and requires businesses to implement reasonable data security measures. The New York Consumer Protection Act (GBL § 349) prohibits deceptive acts and practices, with a private right of action for consumers. The New York Attorney General has an active consumer protection division that has pursued major cases against banks, telecoms, and auto dealers. The New York City Consumer and Worker Protection agency enforces additional local consumer rights. New York has a $50 minimum damage award for GBL § 349 violations plus attorney fees.
laws.penalty: SHIELD Act violation: civil penalty up to $250,000; GBL § 349 violation: $50 minimum + attorney fees per violation
exceptions: SHIELD Act applies to any business with NY residents' data
Private right of action under GBL 349 with attorney fees
laws.source: N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 349; SHIELD Act (2019)
laws.sourceLabel: New York SHIELD Act & Consumer Rights

quiz.q: What does New York's GBL § 349 provide consumers who successfully sue for deceptive practices?
quiz.explanation: New York's General Business Law § 349 provides consumers who succeed in deceptive practices claims a minimum of $50 in damages (even without proving actual harm) plus attorney fees, making it easier to bring small consumer protection cases.

laws.title: SAFE Act — NY Secure Ammunition and Firearms Enforcement
laws.subtitle: NY SAFE Act (2013) — expanded assault weapon ban
laws.fullDescription: New York's SAFE Act (2013), enacted after Sandy Hook, expanded the state's assault weapon ban to include semi-automatic rifles/shotguns with ONE (previously two) military-style feature. It requires universal background checks for ammunition purchases, bans magazines over 7 rounds (later enjoined), requires background checks for private sales, and mandates mental health reporting for firearm eligibility. NY also requires annual re-certification of handgun licenses.
laws.penalty: Possession of assault weapon: class D felony (up to 7 years). Illegal magazine: class A misdemeanor.
exceptions: Law enforcement exempt
Pre-ban weapons may be grandfathered with registration
Antique firearms exempt from some provisions

quiz.q: Under New York's SAFE Act, what number of prohibited features makes a semi-automatic rifle an 'assault weapon'?
quiz.explanation: NY's SAFE Act (2013) tightened the assault weapon definition from requiring TWO prohibited features to just ONE. Features include pistol grips, telescoping stocks, thumbhole stocks, and grenade launcher mounts on semi-automatic centerfire rifles.

laws.title: Stop-and-Frisk — Terry Stop Limits
laws.subtitle: Floyd v. City of New York (2013) — ruled unconstitutional as practiced
laws.fullDescription: New York City's 'stop-and-frisk' program allowed police to stop, question, and frisk individuals based on 'reasonable suspicion.' At its peak in 2011, NYPD conducted 685,000 stops — 88% were Black or Latino and 88% were innocent. Federal Judge Scheindlin ruled in Floyd v. NYC (2013) that the program as practiced violated the 4th and 14th Amendments (unconstitutional racial profiling). Mayor de Blasio dropped the city's appeal. Stops fell from 685,000 (2011) to 13,459 (2019).
laws.penalty: Unconstitutional stops: evidence suppression, civil liability, civil rights lawsuits. Officers may face discipline.
exceptions: Terry stops remain legal when based on individualized, articulable reasonable suspicion
Frisk permitted if officer reasonably believes subject armed and dangerous
Not all pedestrian stops are unconstitutional — Floyd addressed the pattern, not individual stops
laws.sourceLabel: NYPD — Stop, Question and Frisk Data

quiz.q: In the peak year of NYPD's stop-and-frisk program (2011), how many stops were conducted?
quiz.explanation: NYPD conducted 685,724 stops in 2011 — the peak year of the stop-and-frisk program. Federal Judge Scheindlin ruled the program as practiced unconstitutional in Floyd v. NYC (2013), finding it constituted racial profiling in violation of the 4th and 14th Amendments.

laws.title: NY Paid Family Leave — Strongest in US
laws.subtitle: NYPFL — up to 67% wages for 12 weeks
laws.fullDescription: New York's Paid Family Leave (PFL) law provides eligible employees up to 12 weeks of paid leave at 67% of their average weekly wage (capped at 67% of the statewide average). PFL covers bonding with a newborn/adopted child, caring for a seriously ill family member, or qualifying military exigencies. It is employee-funded through payroll deduction (~$0.60-$1/week). New York's PFL is among the most comprehensive in the US.
laws.penalty: Employer retaliation for taking PFL: civil damages, reinstatement, attorney's fees. Carrier denial: appeal rights to NY Workers' Comp Board.
exceptions: Employees must work 26+ consecutive weeks (full-time) or 175 days (part-time) for eligibility
Self-employed may opt in voluntarily
Federal employees covered separately under FMLA
laws.sourceLabel: New York State Paid Family Leave

quiz.q: Under New York's Paid Family Leave law, what percentage of wages does it replace up to 12 weeks?
quiz.explanation: New York's PFL provides up to 67% of an employee's average weekly wage (capped at 67% of the statewide average wage) for up to 12 weeks. This is among the highest wage replacement rates in the US and is fully employee-funded through small payroll deductions.

laws.title: Rent Stabilization — NYC's 1 Million Rent-Regulated Units
laws.subtitle: NYC Rent Stabilization Law covering ~45% of apartments
laws.fullDescription: New York City has the most extensive rent regulation system in the US, covering approximately 1 million apartments (about 45% of the rental market). Rent-stabilized apartments (built 1974-1996 or converted) have regulated rents with annual increases set by the Rent Guidelines Board. Rent-controlled apartments (older, longer-tenancy) have even stricter caps. The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (2019) strengthened tenant protections, eliminated most 'vacancy bonuses' and 'individual apartment improvements' loopholes.
laws.penalty: Illegal rent overcharge: penalty of 2x overcharge (treble damages for willful violations). Harassment to vacate: civil and criminal liability.
exceptions: Buildings with fewer than 6 units pre-1974 may be exempt
Luxury units above rent threshold deregulated
Owner-occupied 1-2 family homes exempt

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New York City's rental market is rent-regulated?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 45% of New York City's rental apartments — about 1 million units — are rent-regulated (either rent-stabilized or rent-controlled). This represents the largest concentration of rent-regulated housing in the United States.

laws.title: NY Human Rights Law — Broadest US Civil Rights Statute
laws.subtitle: NYSHRL covers all employers regardless of size
laws.fullDescription: The New York State Human Rights Law (NYSHRL) prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, credit, and public accommodations based on protected characteristics. Unlike federal law (Title VII requires 15+ employees), NYSHRL covers all employers regardless of size. The 2019 amendments expanded protections: eliminated the 'severe or pervasive' standard for harassment, extended statute of limitations to 3 years, and allowed damages without physical injury. NYC's Human Rights Law provides additional broader protections.
laws.penalty: Violations: back pay, compensatory damages, punitive damages (no cap), attorney's fees, civil penalties up to $100,000.
exceptions: Religious institutions may prefer coreligionists in employment
Bona fide occupational qualifications (BFOQ) defense available
Small nonprofits have some modified requirements

quiz.q: How does New York's Human Rights Law differ from federal Title VII regarding employer size?
options: NYSHRL only covers employers with 50+ employees
NYSHRL covers all employers regardless of size
NYSHRL requires 5+ employees vs Title VII's 15
NYSHRL and Title VII have identical employer size thresholds
quiz.explanation: New York's Human Rights Law covers all employers regardless of size, while federal Title VII only applies to employers with 15 or more employees. This means a New York business with 2 employees is covered by the NYSHRL but not federal anti-discrimination law.

laws.title: Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
laws.subtitle: CLCPA (2019) — 70% renewable by 2030, net-zero by 2050
laws.fullDescription: New York's CLCPA (2019) is one of the world's most ambitious climate laws: 70% renewable electricity by 2030, 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040, economy-wide net-zero emissions by 2050. It established the Climate Action Council to develop a scoping plan. Environmental justice provisions require 35-40% of benefits to go to disadvantaged communities. The law created the Climate Justice Working Group. Offshore wind targets include 9 GW by 2035.
laws.penalty: State agencies must comply with CLCPA when making decisions. Failure to implement: judicial review, agency accountability.
exceptions: Some industrial processes may have extended timelines
Natural gas for reliability may be permitted during transition
Native American territories have sovereign jurisdiction

quiz.q: What is New York's CLCPA electricity target for 2030?
quiz.explanation: The CLCPA requires 70% of New York's electricity to come from renewable sources by 2030, followed by 100% zero-emission electricity by 2040, and economy-wide net-zero emissions by 2050.

laws.title: Rockefeller Drug Laws — Reform History
laws.subtitle: Mandatory minimums reformed by DLRA (2009)
laws.fullDescription: New York's Rockefeller Drug Laws (1973) established some of America's harshest mandatory minimum sentences: 15 years to life for possessing 4+ oz. of heroin/cocaine. The laws were criticized as disproportionately affecting minorities and non-violent offenders. The Drug Law Reform Act (2009) eliminated most mandatory minimums for drug offenses and allowed resentencing for thousands already imprisoned. DLRA 2009 shifted to judicial discretion. New York continued marijuana reform with adult legalization in 2021 (MRTA).
laws.penalty: Post-2009: drug sales/possession sentences based on judicial discretion within revised ranges. A-I felony (most serious): still carries 8-20 years.
exceptions: Major drug traffickers may still receive enhanced sentences
Juvenile drug offenses handled in Family Court
Drug court diversion programs available as alternative
laws.sourceLabel: NY Division of Criminal Justice Services

quiz.q: What mandatory minimum sentence did the original Rockefeller Drug Laws set for possessing 4+ ounces of heroin?
quiz.explanation: New York's Rockefeller Drug Laws (1973) set a mandatory minimum of 15 years to life for possessing 4 or more ounces of heroin or cocaine — regardless of the individual's role or history. These laws were widely criticized as disproportionate and were significantly reformed by the Drug Law Reform Act (2009).

laws.title: NY Legalized Sports Betting — Online Gambling
laws.subtitle: New York's mobile sports betting launched January 2022
laws.fullDescription: New York legalized mobile/online sports betting in January 2022, becoming one of the largest sports betting markets in the US. New York charges the highest sports betting tax rate in the nation — 51% of operator gross gaming revenue. Despite the high tax, major operators (DraftKings, FanDuel, Caesars) participate due to New York's massive market. In-person betting at casinos was already legal. Online poker and other online casino gambling remain illegal. New York generated over $800 million in tax revenue from sports betting in its first year.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed sports betting: criminal prosecution, fines. Operators: license revocation. Problem gambling resources mandatory.
exceptions: Daily fantasy sports operate under separate regulatory framework
Horseracing wagering governed by Racing and Wagering Board
Native American tribal casinos operate under separate compacts

quiz.q: What sports betting tax rate does New York charge operators — the highest in the US?
quiz.explanation: New York charges a 51% tax on sports betting operator gross gaming revenue — the highest rate in the United States. Despite this, major operators participate due to New York's large population. The state generated over $800 million in tax revenue in its first year.

laws.title: Congestion Pricing — NYC MTA (2024)
laws.subtitle: First US congestion pricing zone in Manhattan
laws.fullDescription: New York City launched the first congestion pricing program in the United States in June 2024 — charging drivers entering Manhattan south of 60th Street. Passenger cars pay $9/entry (off-peak $2.25). Trucks pay $14.40-$21.60. The revenue funds the MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority) capital program, primarily for subway and bus improvements. The program was paused in June 2024 by Governor Hochul citing economic concerns, then partially reinstated through legal action.
laws.penalty: Toll violations: $50 fee plus tolls owed. Repeated violations: vehicle registration suspended.
exceptions: Emergency vehicles exempt
Vehicles with disabled placard holders have reduced tolls
Some low-income residents get tax credits
Tunnels (Lincoln, Holland) have credit for toll already paid

quiz.q: What is the base toll for passenger cars entering New York City's congestion pricing zone?
quiz.explanation: New York City's congestion pricing program charges $9 per entry for passenger cars into Manhattan south of 60th Street (off-peak $2.25). The program was the first in the United States and is expected to generate $1 billion annually for MTA capital improvements.

laws.title: Bail Reform — Elimination of Cash Bail for Most Offenses
laws.subtitle: 2019 bail reform eliminates cash bail for non-violent charges
laws.fullDescription: New York's 2019 bail reform eliminated cash bail for most misdemeanors and non-violent felonies, replacing it with supervised release and appearance tickets. The reform was intended to end wealth-based pretrial detention. After public safety concerns, 2020 and 2022 amendments added 'dangerousness' considerations for more serious crimes. Judges gained more discretion to impose cash bail for a broader range of offenses. New York remains more restrictive than most states on cash bail use.
laws.penalty: Bail jumping: class E-D felony (additional charge). Failure to appear: bench warrant issued.
exceptions: Violent felonies, sex offenses, and domestic violence charges may have cash bail
Judges may impose non-monetary conditions (GPS, check-ins)
Defendants with open violent cases may be detained regardless of new charge

quiz.q: What did New York's 2019 bail reform eliminate for most non-violent felonies?
quiz.explanation: New York's 2019 bail reform eliminated cash bail for most misdemeanors and non-violent felonies, replacing pretrial detention with supervised release and appearance tickets. The reform was amended in 2020 and 2022 after public safety concerns to give judges more discretion for certain cases.

laws.title: 421-a Tax Exemption — Affordable Housing
laws.subtitle: 421-a incentivizes affordable units in NYC development
laws.fullDescription: New York's 421-a tax exemption program provides property tax exemptions for residential development in New York City in exchange for including affordable housing units. The program has been central to NYC's development model but criticized for providing large subsidies with modest affordability requirements. The program expired in 2022 and was replaced by 485-x (2024), which requires higher wages for construction workers and deeper affordability — 25% of units at 40% AMI in some areas.
laws.penalty: Failure to maintain affordability requirements: recapture of tax benefits plus interest and penalties.
exceptions: Standalone affordable housing projects may qualify for deeper exemptions
Mixed-income projects have different affordability tier requirements
Projects near transit may have enhanced benefits

quiz.q: What key requirement did New York's 485-x (2024) add compared to 421-a for tax exemptions?
options: Mandatory solar panels on all buildings
Higher wages for construction workers and deeper affordability
quiz.explanation: NY's 485-x (2024) replacement for 421-a requires higher prevailing wages for construction workers in exchange for the tax exemption, as well as deeper affordability requirements in certain areas. This addressed longtime criticism that 421-a provided large tax subsidies without sufficient worker protections.

laws.title: Opioid Crisis — OASAS & Syringe Exchange
laws.subtitle: NY leads in harm reduction — syringe exchange programs
laws.fullDescription: New York has been at the forefront of opioid crisis response, establishing over 150 needle/syringe exchange programs — the most of any state. The programs serve over 100,000 people annually and are credited with significantly reducing HIV rates among IV drug users (from ~50% HIV prevalence in 1990 to <5%). New York also legalized naloxone (Narcan) without prescription and implemented 'Good Samaritan' laws protecting overdose witnesses from arrest. The opioid settlement with manufacturers funds treatment programs.
laws.penalty: Drug possession has been reduced — NY repealed mandatory minimums for possession. Overdose reporting protected by Good Samaritan law.
exceptions: Good Samaritan law protects 911 callers and overdose witnesses from drug possession charges
Naloxone available without prescription
Supervised consumption sites (OPC) opened in NYC in 2021 — first legal sites in US

quiz.q: What was New York City's unique 2021 milestone in opioid harm reduction?
options: First state to legalize all drug use
First legal supervised consumption (overdose prevention) sites in the US
First state to provide free heroin to addicts
First city to decriminalize all drug possession
quiz.explanation: In 2021, New York City opened the first legal supervised consumption sites (Overdose Prevention Centers) in the United States — where people can use pre-obtained drugs under medical supervision with naloxone available. The sites, operated by OnPoint NYC, reported preventing hundreds of overdose deaths in their first year.

laws.title: NY Income Tax — 10.9% Top Rate
laws.subtitle: New York's high income taxes fund state programs
laws.fullDescription: New York State imposes income taxes up to 10.9% on taxable income above $25 million (2021 increase). New York City adds up to 3.876% city income tax. Combined state+city+federal rate for top earners in NYC can exceed 50%. New York's high taxes reflect its extensive social programs and public services. The state relies heavily on high earners — the top 1% pay over 40% of state income taxes, making revenues volatile. Many high earners have claimed migration to Florida or Texas to avoid taxes.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: criminal prosecution, civil penalties, interest. NY audits out-of-state residents who earned NY income.
exceptions: Retirement income partially exempt
Social Security benefits exempt
Military pay exempt for non-resident military
laws.sourceLabel: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance

quiz.q: What is New York State's top income tax rate (2024)?
quiz.explanation: New York State's top marginal income tax rate is 10.9% on taxable income above $25 million. Combined with New York City's top rate of 3.876% and federal taxes, top earners in NYC face combined marginal rates exceeding 50%.

laws.title: Reproductive Rights — Roe Codified in NY Law
laws.subtitle: Reproductive Health Act (2019) — abortion up to 24 weeks
laws.fullDescription: New York's Reproductive Health Act (2019) codified abortion rights into state law before Dobbs, protecting abortion access regardless of federal law changes. The law allows abortion up to 24 weeks (or later for health/life necessity), moved abortion from the criminal code to public health law, and allows non-physicians to perform abortions. After Dobbs (2022), New York became a destination state for abortion access. Proposition 1 (2024) added the Equal Rights Amendment to the NY Constitution, including reproductive rights.
laws.penalty: No penalties for patients. Providers operating outside licensed facilities or beyond legal parameters face licensing and criminal liability.
exceptions: Abortions after 24 weeks permitted for health/life of pregnant person
No mandatory waiting periods in New York
Medicaid covers abortion in New York

quiz.q: Up to what gestational age does New York's Reproductive Health Act generally permit abortion?
quiz.explanation: New York's Reproductive Health Act (2019) allows abortion up to 24 weeks of pregnancy. After 24 weeks, abortion remains legal if necessary to protect the health or life of the pregnant person. After Dobbs (2022), New York became a major destination for abortion access from other states.

laws.title: NYC ID Card — IDNYC Program
laws.subtitle: Municipal ID for all NYC residents regardless of immigration status
laws.fullDescription: New York City's IDNYC program (launched 2015) provides free photo ID cards to all NYC residents, including undocumented immigrants. Over 1 million cards have been issued. IDNYC is accepted at city agencies, schools, hospitals, and by major banks. The program provides a form of official identification to undocumented residents who cannot obtain driver's licenses. IDNYC also offered cultural institution memberships and other benefits. ICE does not accept IDNYC as proof of lawful status.
laws.penalty: No penalties related to the IDNYC card itself. Data privacy: NYC law limits sharing IDNYC enrollment data with federal agencies.
exceptions: IDNYC is municipal — not accepted by TSA, federal agencies, or for voting
Not a substitute for driver's license or passport
Some employers may require federal work authorization documents

quiz.q: Who is eligible to obtain New York City's IDNYC card?
options: Only US citizens and legal permanent residents
All New York City residents, including undocumented immigrants
Anyone who pays NYC income tax
Only those over 18 with a bank account
quiz.explanation: IDNYC is available to all New York City residents 10 years and older, regardless of immigration status, national origin, or housing situation. Over 1 million cards have been issued. The program provides official identification to undocumented residents and others who lack government-issued ID.

laws.title: CUNY Free Tuition — Excelsior Scholarship
laws.subtitle: Excelsior Scholarship provides free SUNY/CUNY tuition
laws.fullDescription: New York's Excelsior Scholarship (2017) provides free tuition at SUNY and CUNY institutions for students from families earning up to $125,000/year. Recipients must live and work in New York for the number of years they received the scholarship. Over 60,000 students receive the scholarship annually. New York also has separate Tuition Assistance Program (TAP) grants and opportunity programs (EOP, SEEK, HEOP) for low-income students. Critics note the income threshold favors middle-class families.
laws.penalty: Recipients who leave NY before fulfilling residency requirement: scholarship converts to loan, must repay.
exceptions: Community colleges may be fully covered without residency obligation
Students pursuing in-demand fields may have modified requirements
Students with documented hardship may seek waivers

quiz.q: What is the family income limit for New York's Excelsior Scholarship?
quiz.explanation: New York's Excelsior Scholarship covers tuition at SUNY and CUNY for students from families earning up to $125,000/year. Recipients must live and work in New York state for the same number of years they received the scholarship, or it converts to a repayable loan.

laws.title: Prisoners' Rights — Humane Alternatives to Long-Term Solitary
laws.subtitle: HALT Solitary Confinement Act (2021)
laws.fullDescription: New York's HALT Solitary Confinement Act (2021) — Humane Alternatives to Long-Term Solitary Confinement — phased out solitary confinement in state prisons and jails. The law limits isolated confinement to no more than 15 consecutive days (or 20 days in 60 days for serious misconduct), bans solitary for vulnerable populations (under 21, over 55, pregnant, mental illness, developmental disabilities), and requires alternatives focusing on programming and rehabilitation. New York became the first state to enact such comprehensive limits on solitary.
laws.penalty: DOC violations: audit findings, potential civil liability. Individuals in unlawful isolation: right to relief.
exceptions: Temporary confinement (up to 4 hours) for immediate safety still permitted
Residential mental health units (RMHU) as alternative
Emergency provisions for active violent incidents

quiz.q: Under New York's HALT Act, what is the maximum consecutive days of solitary confinement permitted?
quiz.explanation: New York's HALT Act limits isolated confinement to 15 consecutive days, or 20 days out of any 60-day period for the most serious misconduct. The law also bans solitary entirely for vulnerable populations including those under 21, over 55, pregnant individuals, and those with mental illness.

laws.title: NYC Water Supply — Catskill Watershed Protections
laws.subtitle: NYC unfiltered surface water from protected Catskill watershed
laws.fullDescription: New York City's water supply — one of the largest unfiltered surface water systems in the world — comes from Catskill/Delaware and Croton watersheds supplying 1.1 billion gallons daily to 9 million people. The DEP maintains watershed protections through land purchases, agricultural best practices, and stream buffers, avoiding the $10 billion cost of a filtration plant. The filtration avoidance determination (FAD) from EPA requires NY to maintain water quality standards through watershed protection.
laws.penalty: Watershed violations (prohibited activities in buffer zones, agricultural runoff): fines, enforcement orders, loss of FAD requiring filtration plant construction.
exceptions: The Croton system requires filtration (completed 2012)
Some upstate communities use local wells or springs
DEP purchases watershed land from willing sellers only

quiz.q: What is the daily volume of water New York City's watershed system supplies to 9 million people?
quiz.explanation: NYC's Catskill/Delaware and Croton watersheds supply approximately 1.1 billion gallons of drinking water daily to about 9 million people. NYC maintains one of the few large unfiltered surface water systems in the US through rigorous watershed protection programs.

laws.title: Community Reinvestment Act — NY Banking Compliance
laws.subtitle: CRA requires banks to serve low-income NY communities
laws.fullDescription: The federal Community Reinvestment Act (CRA, 1977) requires banks to meet the credit needs of low-income and minority communities in their service areas. New York's Department of Financial Services (DFS) enforces CRA obligations for state-chartered banks and has extended CRA-like requirements to non-bank lenders. NYC's DFS has issued consumer financial protection regulations including payday lending restrictions, debt collection rules, and mortgage servicing standards. New York also banned discriminatory insurance redlining.
laws.penalty: Poor CRA ratings can block bank mergers/acquisitions. DFS enforcement: civil fines, required remediation plans. Illegal redlining: civil rights lawsuits.
exceptions: Small banks have streamlined CRA examinations
Credit unions exempt from CRA (but subject to similar regulations)
Community development banks receive CRA credit for all activities

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act?
options: Requiring banks to invest in government bonds
Requiring banks to meet credit needs of low-income communities
quiz.explanation: The CRA (1977) requires banks to demonstrate they are meeting the credit needs of low- and moderate-income communities in their service areas. CRA ratings affect bank merger approvals and are a tool to combat redlining and disinvestment in underserved communities.

laws.title: Marriage Equality — NY Marriage Equality Act (2011)
laws.subtitle: NY legalized same-sex marriage before federal Obergefell
laws.fullDescription: New York legalized same-sex marriage through the Marriage Equality Act (2011) — one of the largest states to do so before the Supreme Court's Obergefell v. Hodges decision (2015). The law passed the Senate 33-29 with Republican support from Governor Cuomo's outreach. New York has performed over 50,000 same-sex marriages. After Obergefell, New York's law was superseded by federal constitutional right but remains in state law. New York also recognized out-of-state same-sex marriages before state legalization.
laws.penalty: Denying marriage services based on sexual orientation: discrimination law violations. County clerks may not refuse to issue licenses.
exceptions: Religious organizations may decline to perform ceremonies
Religious officiants have First Amendment protections for ceremony refusal
Religious nonprofits may have exemptions for employment

quiz.q: In what year did New York legalize same-sex marriage through the Marriage Equality Act?
quiz.explanation: New York legalized same-sex marriage through the Marriage Equality Act in 2011 — four years before the Supreme Court's Obergefell v. Hodges decision (2015) made same-sex marriage a constitutional right nationwide. New York was the sixth and largest state to legalize same-sex marriage.
